papers.abstract: Metastatic progression is a major cause of colorectal cancer (CRC)-related mortality, but the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of lysine-specific demethylase 1A (KDM1A) in CRC metastasis and angiogenesis-related phenotypes. Using transcriptomic profiling, chromatin immunoprecipitation, functional assays, and preclinical models, we found that KDM1A contributes to CRC cell migration, invasion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), with NRP2 upregulation serving as an important associated mechanism. Mechanistically, KDM1A was associated with reduced enrichment of H3K9me1/2 at the NRP2 regulatory region, supporting a chromatin-associated mechanism for NRP2 transcriptional regulation. TGF-β/Smad signaling may also provide an auxiliary input to NRP2 expression. In parallel, KDM1A increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) protein stability and VEGFA expression, thereby contributing to angiogenesis-related activity. Our data further suggest that NRP2 and VEGFA-related signaling are linked to PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation and metastatic phenotypes in CRC cells. Pharmacological inhibition of KDM1A with GSK-LSD1 reduced liver metastatic burden and vascularization within metastatic lesions in preclinical models. Together, these findings suggest that KDM1A contributes to CRC metastatic progression through related mechanisms involving NRP2 regulation, HIF-1α/VEGFA-associated angiogenesis, and AKT pathway modulation, providing a basis for further investigation of KDM1A as a potential therapeutic target in metastatic CRC.

papers.abstract: Abstract Hyperactivation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, is common in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, clinical use of mTOR inhibitors has shown limited efficacy due to rapid adaptive resistance. Using inducible genetically engineered mouse models and matched organoids, we delineated distinct complex-specific adaptations. Loss of mTORC1 delayed tumor progression but induced compensatory PI3K/Akt signalling hyperactivation, while concurrently suppressing inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts and desmoplasia through Il-1ra. In contrast, mTORC2 loss impaired de novo sphingolipid synthesis, shifted lipid composition toward saturation, increased the saturated-to-monounsaturated fatty acid ratio, enriched plasma membrane lipid rafts, and amplified interferon-γ signaling. This lipid reprogramming generated a synthetic-lethal dependency on stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (Scd1). Pharmacological co-inhibition of mTORC1/2 and Scd1 prevented adaptive PI3K/Akt signalling rebound, remodelled the tumor stroma, enhanced interferon-γ responses, and synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy. These findings establish dual targeting of mTOR signaling and Scd1 as a rational therapeutic strategy for PDAC.

papers.abstract: Specific genetic mutations serve as clues to cancer emergence. However, non-genetic cell state shift mechanisms-such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-drive swift, reversible drug tolerance and metastasis. Unlike the slow process of acquiring mutations, this plasticity allows rapid, drug-tolerant cells to revert to previous states upon withdrawal of the drug, thereby driving pharmacological resistance. Insight into the evolution of cell states in cancer is critical for optimizing drug regimens. Here we propose dynamic conformational heterogeneity as an untapped fundamental driver of adaptive resistance. Proteins do not function as simple binary switches; rather, they exist as dynamic ensembles. Cancer arises when their conformational distribution shifts permanently towards an active state. Drugs operate by selecting specific (oncogenic) 3D conformer shapes and reverse-shifting the population back to a stabilized inactive state. Epigenetic dysregulation in cancer cells amplifies expression levels of these proteins, shifting the ensemble toward the oncogenic state. The increased abundance of the active state saturates the networks, overcoming feedback controls. We propose that effectively countering cancer evolution requires drug combinations that target oncogenic conformations at both molecular and systems levels, including adaptive phenotypic plasticity factors, shifting focus from individual static targets to dynamic population states.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Seychelles, the smallest country in Africa but with the highest GDP per capita, has experienced rapid socioeconomic development. We analysed 20‐year cancer incidence trends (2005–2024) using data from the Seychelles National Cancer Registry (SNCR). Annual age‐standardised incidence rates (ASRs), average annual percentage changes (AAPCs), and stage at diagnosis (for the four major cancers) were calculated. Incidence rates for the most recent decade (2015–2024) were also compared with those in selected African countries and high Human Development Index (HDI) countries. Among men, prostate cancer had the highest incidence (ASR 73.9 per 100,000) and increased significantly over time (AAPC +6.7%), reaching an ASR of 90.3 per 100,000 in 2015–2024. Significant declines were observed for oesophageal (AAPC −4.3%) and laryngeal cancers (AAPC −5.6%). Among women, breast cancer was the most common cancer (ASR 54.7 per 100,000), increasing by 3.4% annually and reaching an ASR of 70.5 per 100,000 in the most recent decade, comparable to rates in Europe. Significant increases were also observed for colorectal, cervical, and corpus uteri cancers. The observed trends reflect Seychelles' epidemiological transition, with a shift from infection‐related cancers towards cancers associated with ageing and lifestyle factors, resembling the cancer profile of high‐income countries. Nevertheless, the major cancers—prostate, breast, colorectal, and cervical—continue to be diagnosed at relatively advanced stages, highlighting the need for improved early detection and timely diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Abstract Early detection of cancer remains one of the most effective strategies to reduce cancer mortality. Artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance existing cancer screening across modalities by improving testing performance (e.g., accuracy, sensitivity, specificity), reducing false positives and negatives, automating workflows, and enabling risk-based care. However, accurate, robust, generalizable AI requires large, diverse, well-annotated datasets that are difficult to centralize because of privacy regulations, institutional governance, and heterogeneous infrastructure. Federated learning (FL) addresses this constraint by training models across institutions without transferring patient data. Through secure aggregation and differential privacy, FL preserves confidentiality while enabling collaboration. Early studies in breast, lung, and cervical screening report that FL can approach centralized performance and improve cross-site generalization; however, most rely on simulated clients, few participating sites, and limited external validation, so these findings should be regarded as preliminary rather than established. Critically, FL is not a shortcut to rigorous results, and heterogeneous, variably curated data demand intensive cleaning and quality control, which are central barriers to reliable implementation. In this review, we synthesize the state of FL for early cancer detection across imaging, digital pathology, multi-omics, and clinical data; outline core FL concepts and privacy technologies; and summarize applications by cancer type. We critically examine regulatory, operational, and translational barriers that currently limit clinical adoption. Finally, we propose a practical roadmap, which is centered on multimodal and longitudinal FL, foundation-model-enabled adaptation, prospective evaluation within clinical workflows, and equitable participation of community and low-resource sites, to advance privacy-preserving, generalizable AI for population-scale cancer screening.

papers.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 3 (CDKN3), also known as kinase-associated phosphatase (KAP), dephosphorylates activating cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) Thr160, yet high expression is associated with aggressive features in some cancers. This review distinguishes messenger RNA (mRNA) expression, protein abundance, phosphatase activity, functional dependency, prognostic association, and treatment-response prediction. Renal studies include selected perturbation evidence, whereas lung studies cited here primarily report prognostic or computational associations. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) findings remain directionally discordant across analytes, etiologies, models, and endpoints. Recent triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) studies include transcriptomic and cell-perturbation evidence, as well as a separate cell and murine mammary fat-pad graft study, while an ultraviolet (UV)-induced skin-cancer study identifies a sex- and context-specific protective axis. These results do not support a universal CDKN3 role. A CDKN3-specific connection to chromosomal instability (CIN) and cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling remains unvalidated. Micronuclei and CIN do not invariably activate cGAS–STING. Bulk immune signatures and survival associations alone cannot establish direct immune regulation, functional dependency, or treatment sensitivity. This focused narrative review compares molecular measurements, genetic perturbations, clinical associations, and selected computational studies. We outline matched assays, genetic rescue, longitudinal CIN measurements, and pathway-specific tests needed to determine whether CDKN3 is a context-specific dependency, a biomarker, or a therapeutic target.

papers.abstract: Background Deep tabular models, including self-supervised and pretrained foundation models, are increasingly proposed for clinical risk prediction, but their value over conventional learners is rarely tested against matched controls, and their role relative to clinician judgement is seldom examined. Methods In a retrospective single-centre cohort of 879 women referred for colposcopy (242 CIN2+, 27.5%), 15 routinely recorded variables, including a clinician image-based assessment documented before histopathology, were modelled with ten model families under one fixed protocol (single fold assignment and seed, no tuning). Discrimination was compared by paired DeLong tests and bootstrap. Two analyses were pre-specified: exact Shapley attribution of discrimination to five clinical groups of variables in every model family, and a complementarity analysis asking whether routine data identify CIN2+ among women judged negative by the clinician. Frozen models were evaluated in a 103-case two-centre external cohort. Results Out-of-fold AUROC ranged from 0.726 to 0.761. No model outperformed logistic regression (AUROC 0.757; CatBoost −0.002, p = 0.860; TabPFN +0.004, p = 0.554), and three matched ablations of a self-supervised tabular Transformer were null (all p ≥ 0.096). Removing the clinician assessment lowered AUROC in all ten families (by 0.041 to 0.072; all p ≤ 0.008). Shapley attribution ranked five variable groups identically in every family (Kendall’s W = 1.00; permutation p < 0.001): the clinician assessment (39% to 50% of discrimination above chance), then cytology, HPV testing, colposcopic findings and demographic history. The clinician assessment alone had sensitivity 0.504 and specificity 0.882; 49.6% of CIN2+ occurred in clinician-negative women. Re-reviewing the 20% of clinician-negative women with the highest model risk identified 34.2% (95% CI 25.7–42.7%) of the missed CIN2+, against 20% expected at random, raising pathway sensitivity to 0.674 at specificity 0.733. External AUROC of logistic regression was 0.710. Conclusions On routine structured data from a colposcopy-referral population, and under a common protocol, model architecture did not determine performance; predictor information did. Retrospectively, routine data complemented the clinician modestly in clinician-negative women, rather than replacing clinical judgement. Claims that complex architectures improve clinical tabular prediction should be tested against logistic regression with paired uncertainty across repeated data splits.

papers.abstract: Introduction Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive and diverse subtype of breast cancer with few therapeutic choices and poor prognosis. This is mostly because of recurrence, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Members of the tripartite motif-containing protein family (TRIM) have emerged as significant regulators of tumor growth due to their functions in cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and metastasis. TRIM33 has been shown to operate context-dependently as either a tumor suppressor or a tumor promoter in various cancers, partly because of its participation in TGF-β-related signaling pathways. However, little is known about the expression pattern and epigenetic regulation of TRIM33 in TNBC, especially in Indian patients. Methods Twenty-eight patients with histologically confirmed TNBC were included in the study. Tumor tissue and paired adjacent non-tumor breast tissue were collected at the time of surgery. TRIM33 mRNA and protein expression were evaluated using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. TRIM33 promoter methylation status was assessed using methylation-specific PCR (MS-PCR). Results TRIM33 expression was increased in TNBC tissue compared with paired adjacent non-tumor tissue. Increased TRIM33 mRNA expression was observed in 19 of 28 cases (67.9%), while elevated TRIM33 protein expression was detected in 16 of 28 cases (57.1%). An unmethylated/hypomethylated TRIM33 promoter pattern was observed in 22 of 28 cases (78.6%).TRIM33 protein expression showed significant associations with selected clinicopathological characteristics, including clinical stage. Promoter methylation status was also associated with selected clinicopathological parameters. Conclusion Promoter hypomethylation of TRIM33 was frequently observed in TNBC and was associated with increased TRIM33 expression and selected clinicopathological characteristics. These findings suggest a potential role for epigenetic regulation of TRIM33 in TNBC and warrant validation in larger patient cohorts.

papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs) in Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1) are typically multifocal, small-bowel-based, and wild-type for KIT and PDGFRA, so surgery remains the cornerstone of treatment. Multifocal duodeno-jejunal involvement poses technical and strategic challenges, and minimally invasive management in this setting is poorly standardized. We describe a hybrid laparoscopic–mini-open, bowel-preserving approach. Laparoscopic access via the Hasson technique with three additional trocars allows systematic small-bowel exploration. Division of the ligament of Treitz and a complete Kocher maneuver fully mobilize the duodeno-pancreatic block. Targeted lesions are exteriorized through a short Alexis-protected minilaparotomy and removed by manual full-thickness wedge resection with double-layer closure. A selective strategy is applied: only enlarging or anatomically critical lesions are resected, while subcentimeter micro-GISTs are left in situ . In a 62-year-old man with NF1 and three growing GISTs (duodenal and jejunal), all targeted lesions were resected with negative (R0) margins. Histology confirmed low-risk and no risk tumors. Recovery was uneventful aside from transient delayed gastric emptying, and the patient was recurrence-free at 12 months. This standardized, reproducible technique provides a tailored minimally invasive option for multifocal NF1-associated GISTs, preserving bowel length without compromising oncologic adequacy.

papers.abstract: Background Readiness for stoma reversal is an important concept for patients with a diverting stoma during the transition from “living with a stoma” to “resumption of transanal defecation and adaptation to postoperative bowel function.” However, its conceptual meaning remains unclear, limiting the development of related research and clinical practice. Therefore, it is necessary to clearly define the concept of readiness for stoma reversal in patients with a diverting stoma. Objective To clarify the concept of readiness for stoma reversal in patients with a diverting stoma using Rodgers’ evolutionary concept analysis. Methods Relevant studies on readiness for stoma reversal in patients with a diverting stoma were systematically searched in PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and VIP Database. Rodgers’ evolutionary concept analysis was used to synthesize and analyze the included studies. The conceptual attributes, antecedents, consequences, and related concepts of readiness for stoma reversal in patients with a diverting stoma were extracted and summarized. Results The core attributes of readiness for stoma reversal in patients with a diverting stoma include pre-reversal assessment, physical and functional readiness, information and knowledge readiness, and psychological readiness. The main antecedents included rectal cancer control and anastomotic healing, systematic health education and health literacy, socioeconomic conditions and support systems, and multidisciplinary assessment and collaboration. For patients, adequate readiness may facilitate bowel function recovery, enhance engagement in rehabilitation and self-management, reduce anxiety and fear, lower the risk of postoperative complications, and improve quality of life. For healthcare systems, it may help shorten hospital stays, reduce readmissions and other unplanned healthcare use, and lower related medical costs. Conclusion Readiness for stoma reversal is a multidimensional and dynamic state that develops before reversal in patients with a diverting stoma. It reflects the patient’s ability to cope with stoma reversal, bowel function recovery after reversal, and related lifestyle changes. Clarifying the attributes, antecedents, and consequences of this concept may support the development of assessment tools for readiness for stoma reversal. It may also provide a basis for designing individualized and continuous nursing interventions.

papers.abstract: Aim To investigate the predictive value of dynamic heart rate variability (HRV) changes during the perioperative period for complications following radical surgery for gastrointestinal tumors. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 231 patients who underwent elective radical surgery for gastrointestinal tumors at the Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine between May 2022 and September 2025. Based on the occurrence of complications during postoperative hospitalization, they were divided into a complication group (n = 41) and a non-complication group (n = 190). All patients wore a long-term wearable dynamic monitoring device recording dynamic heart rate variability indicators from 24 hours preoperatively to postoperative day 3. Concurrent changes in inflammatory markers were also recorded. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to construct prediction models, and receiver operating characteristic curves were plotted to evaluate their predictive performance. Results The root mean square of successive differences on postoperative day 3 was significantly lower in the complication group than in the non-complication group, while the low-frequency/high-frequency ratio was higher and recovered slowly. Among the inflammatory markers, interleukin-6, white blood cell, and C-reactive protein levels were significantly higher in the complication group. The combined model incorporating heart rate variability trajectory parameters and serum markers demonstrated the highest predictive value (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.832, 95% CI: 0.762–0.902, P < 0.001). Conclusion Dynamic perioperative HRV monitoring can effectively reflect the state of autonomic function under surgical stress. By combining HRV with inflammatory markers, we established the model to identify the association between HRV and the risk of short-term postoperative complications, thereby facilitating the early identification and intervention of high-risk patients.

papers.abstract: Objective This study investigated the distribution and maturity of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in invasive breast carcinoma tissue, as well as their prognostic value for postoperative recurrence. Methods This study retrospectively collected tissue samples from 127 patients with invasive breast carcinoma at the Second People’s Hospital of Guangdong Province between January 2021 and December 2023. Immunohistochemistry was conducted to measure TLS and the expression of related proteins in invasive breast carcinoma and peritumoral tissues. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to determine the association between TLS and postoperative recurrence during the follow-up period. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed to evaluate the discriminatory performance of TLS for postoperative recurrence. Results The number and grade of TLS in invasive breast carcinoma tissue, as well as CD155 and Ki-67 expression, were markedly higher than those in peritumoral tissue. Compared with the non-recurrence group, patients in the recurrence group had a decreased number and grade of TLS in their tumor tissue and exhibited higher CD155 and Ki-67 expression intensity. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that breast-conserving surgery, high CD155 expression, and high Ki-67 expression were independent positive predictors of postoperative recurrence, whereas a higher TLS grade was an independent negative predictor. TLS grade demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.740, a sensitivity of 91.30%, and a specificity of 56.70%. Conclusion TLS presence in invasive breast carcinoma tissue and its maturity level are negatively associated with recurrence risk, serving as a potential prognostic marker for recurrence in patients with invasive breast carcinoma.

papers.abstract: Intracranial dose constraints are often treated as fixed properties of neural tissue, yet their meaning depends on the metric, volume definition, source population and clinical time horizon in which they were derived. In IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, these conditions may differ from current planning practice. We identify three potential discontinuities: non-equivalent dose metrics may be treated as interchangeable; volume- or subregion-specific recommendations may be collapsed into single organ-level limits; and thresholds derived in longer-surviving populations may be transferred to a disease in which competing mortality may precede several late endpoints. The brainstem illustrates the metrological problem particularly clearly, whereas the hippocampus and subventricular/periventricular regions illustrate the problem of disease-specific validation. We propose a structure-specific framework with three operations: evaluation of each constraint in its source metric and anatomical definition; classification of each objective by predefined criteria of evidentiary status, endpoint severity and latency, which separates established limits from optimisation objectives; and explicit documentation of any target-coverage trade-off. No new numerical thresholds are proposed, and prognosis never justifies exceeding an established limit. Constraints protecting against severe irreversible injury, including those for the optic nerves and chiasm, are not reassessed.

papers.abstract: Background TNM stage and pretreatment plasma Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA are central to risk assessment in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), but they do not fully capture host metabolic reserve. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 160 patients with non-metastatic NPC treated from 2013 to 2022. The integrated metabolic vulnerability score (IMVS; range, 0-3) assigned 1 point each for stage IVA, triglyceride-to-HDL cholesterol ratio <1.217, and body mass index <23.79 kg/m2. Cox regression and bootstrap internal validation evaluated progression-free survival (PFS), with EBV DNA included as an adjustment variable. A broader 271-patient cohort from the same institution was used only for internal sensitivity analysis. Results Thirty-three PFS events occurred in the modeling cohort. Five-year PFS was 100.0%, 91.9%, 72.1%, and 50.0% for IMVS scores 0, 1, 2, and 3, respectively. IMVS remained associated with PFS after adjustment for EBV DNA status (HR, 2.74; bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 1.89-4.75; P<0.001), although EBV DNA status itself was not independently significant in this cohort. The optimism-corrected AUC was 0.715 for stage IVA, THR, and BMI and 0.727 after adding EBV DNA. In the broader same-institution cohort, the association persisted but was attenuated (HR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.10; P = 0.005). Conclusion IMVS is an exploratory, low-cost risk-stratification tool that may complement, rather than replace, TNM stage and plasma EBV DNA. Prospective external validation and recalibration of the data-derived thresholds are required before clinical use.

papers.abstract: The 3rd International Conference on PEN-Plus in Africa (ICPPA) reaffirmed PEN-Plus’s potential to decentralise care for severe, complex non-communicable diseases and injuries among underserved populations, particularly children and adolescents. Although childhood cancer was recognised as a sentinel condition in the original Lancet Commission report, it has not yet been fully embraced within PEN-Plus implementation. This gap is striking given that nearly 90% of the over 100–000 children who develop cancer annually in sub-Saharan Africa die, largely as a result of underdiagnosis and late-stage presentation. First-level referral hospitals could therefore help bridge primary and tertiary care, improving timely diagnosis, early treatment, and adherence. Accordingly, the next phase of PEN-Plus should be defined not only by expanding coverage to improve access to care, but also by strengthening equitable, child-centred, and integrated service delivery within national primary health care systems and communities – including extending comprehensive services to other orphaned conditions such as childhood cancer.

papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer morbidity and mortality, and metastatic progression, recurrence, chemoresistance, and treatment-related toxicity continue to limit outcomes. Medical ozone has attracted interest as a potential adjunct because, after reacting with biological fluids, it generates short-lived redox mediators such as hydrogen peroxide and lipid oxidation products that may influence NRF2/Keap1, NF-κB, HIF-1α, mitochondrial apoptosis, cytokine signaling, and the tumor microenvironment. However, current CRC-specific evidence is limited and heterogeneous. Experimental studies using CRC cell lines and animal models suggest possible effects on apoptosis, oxidative stress, inflammatory modulation, hypoxia-related pathways, and chemosensitivity, but these findings remain preclinical and are not sufficient to establish antitumor efficacy. Clinical evidence in CRC patients is scarce and mainly relates to supportive care, including radiation-induced rectal injury, chronic treatment-related symptoms, and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, rather than tumor response or survival. Importantly, ozone biology is context dependent: activation of adaptive antioxidant responses may protect normal tissues but could also enhance tumor cell stress tolerance under certain conditions. Route-specific safety is also critical, as inhaled ozone is toxic, whereas non-inhalational approaches require standardized dosing and monitoring. Overall, ozone therapy should be considered an investigational adjunct in CRC, with future studies requiring rigorous trial design, biomarker stratification, standardized administration protocols, and clear separation of anticancer endpoints from symptom-control outcomes.

papers.abstract: Plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) are among the most clinically burdensome tumor manifestations of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and can cause pain, disfigurement, neurological deficits, and compression of vital structures. Their diffuse growth along nerves and blood vessels often limits complete surgical resection. Biallelic NF1 loss results in persistent activation of RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK signaling and provides a strong biological rationale for MEK inhibition. Selumetinib and mirdametinib have received regulatory approval in defined patient populations, while trametinib, luvometinib, and other MEK inhibitors have also demonstrated clinical activity. Nevertheless, responses remain predominantly partial. Some patients show primary nonresponse, limited tumor shrinkage, or treatment-limiting toxicity, and tumor regrowth may occur after dose reduction or treatment discontinuation. This review first summarizes molecular mechanisms and monotherapy evidence, then evaluates rational combinations and their clinical translation. These strategies include vertical inhibition of RAS–MAPK signaling, blockade of parallel survival pathways, targeting of residual tumor-cell states, and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. Combined MEK and SOS1 inhibition has relatively strong PN-specific in vivo support. KRAS–MEK inhibition has emerging mouse-model support, while selumetinib plus cabozantinib is undergoing clinical dose exploration. Strategies targeting CDKs or YAP/TEAD warrant further translational evaluation. In contrast, negative or borderline findings involving SHP2, mTOR, and several microenvironment-directed approaches demonstrate that biological plausibility does not necessarily translate into therapeutic benefit. Because NF1-associated PNs are predominantly benign tumors requiring long-term management, rational combination therapy should not simply increase treatment intensity. Instead, it should address a defined limitation of monotherapy and demonstrate a favorable net clinical benefit over an active single agent. Future treatment may therefore evolve toward mechanism-guided approaches incorporating reduced-dose combinations, sequential or intermittent therapy, rechallenge, and surgery after pharmacological tumor reduction. Tumor volume, pain, function, long-term safety, resectability, and disease control after treatment withdrawal should collectively inform therapeutic value.

papers.abstract: BRCA1-mutant breast cancer is characterized by homologous recombination deficiency and genomic instability. Although these tumors are initially sensitive to platinum-based chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, acquired treatment resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Ferroptosis is a potential therapeutic vulnerability, but the role of the SLC7A11/xCT–ferroptosis axis in this disease remains unclear. Current evidence does not establish whether increased SLC7A11 expression is a causal determinant of platinum- or PARP inhibitor resistance or a secondary response to treatment-induced stress; functional evidence directly linking SLC7A11 manipulation to drug resistance in genotype-defined BRCA1-mutant breast cancer remains limited. This review examines evidence linking SLC7A11-mediated cystine utilization to glutathione synthesis, GPX4-dependent antioxidant defense, redox and metabolic adaptation, and treatment response. We distinguish findings from BRCA1-mutant or BRCA1-deficient models from those in non-stratified breast cancer, TNBC, and broader cancer models, and discuss crosstalk with DNA damage responses and the tumor microenvironment. Individual studies have implicated VDAC3 in erastin response. BRCA1/BARD1-dependent GPX4 regulation has also been linked to ferroptosis control. However, these mechanisms require independent validation. Glucose restriction may produce overlapping but mechanistically separable ferroptotic and disulfidptotic phenotypes in SLC7A11-high cells; direct evidence for disulfidptosis in BRCA1-mutant breast cancer is lacking. Potential therapeutic strategies targeting SLC7A11, NRF2/ATF4 signaling, GPX4-related defenses, NADPH regeneration, glucose metabolism, and stromal or immune–metabolic interactions are reviewed. However, most SLC7A11-centered mechanistic and therapeutic evidence remains preclinical and has not been systematically validated in genotype-defined, platinum- or PARP inhibitor-resistant BRCA1-mutant breast cancer models. Future studies should prioritize biomarker-guided evaluation, pathway-selective experiments to distinguish ferroptosis from disulfidptosis, and prospective validation in treatment-resistant BRCA1-mutant models and clinical cohorts.

papers.abstract: Background Postoperative pneumonia (POP) is a common complication after lung cancer surgery. Numerous risk prediction models for POP have been developed. However, the quality and predictive performance of these models remain unclear. Methods A literature search was carried out in CNKI, Wanfang Database, VIP Database, SinoMed, PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Web of Science. The search covered studies on risk prediction models for postoperative pneumonia in lung cancer patients from inception to July 20, 2026. The research question was formulated using the PICOTS framework. Data extraction was performed following the Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews of Prediction Modelling Studies (CHARMS), and risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Meta-analysis was conducted using STATA 17.0 software. Results A total of 26 prediction models from 20 studies were included. Models were developed predominantly with logistic regression, with machine-learning approaches used in two studies. Common predictors included age, operation time, smoking, diabetes mellitus, preoperative pulmonary function, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and TNM stage. All studies exhibited a high risk of bias, mainly due to inadequate data sources and suboptimal reporting in the analysis domain; 16 studies also raised applicability concerns, mainly due to participant selection limited to specific lung cancer subgroups. The pooled AUC from the meta-analysis was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.87-0.91). Conclusion Although existing postoperative pneumonia prediction models for lung cancer patients show good discriminative performance, their clinical applicability is limited by a high risk of bias, which may lead to overestimation of discrimination. Future studies should develop more robust models with larger sample, rigorous designs, and multicenter external validation. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ , identifier CRD42024554224.

papers.abstract: Background COL1A2 encodes type I collagen alpha2 chain, a stromal component in gastric cancer (GC); its prognostic value, cellular origin, and immune microenvironment relation remain unclear. Methods We analyzed TCGA-STAD, GSE63089, and ACRG GSE62254. Associations between COL1A2 abundance and overall survival (OS), clinicopathology, pathways, and tumor microenvironment were assessed. High/low groups by median expression. Two Cox models used pathological stage or separate T/N/M. Immunotherapy response predicted via TIDE and IPS. WGCNA, PPI, and LASSO with five ECM genes, ten-fold cross-validation and 200 repeats, were applied. qPCR and Western blot measured mRNA and protein in seven paired tissues. Results COL1A2 was higher in GC and linked to poorer OS, but time-dependent AUCs were 0.60, 0.65, 0.66. In ACRG, OS association was not significant (HR 1.83, P = 0.085). Per SD increase, adjusted HR was 1.21 (stage model, P = 0.036) and 1.14 (T/N/M model, P = 0.171). C-index gains were only 0.006 and 0.003. Higher abundance correlated with stroma-rich microenvironment and M2 macrophage infiltration. TIDE/IPS predicted lower ICI response probability. LASSO selected SPARC, ELN, and BGN stably. Tumor tissues showed higher mRNA and protein. Conclusions COL1A2 associates with poor prognosis, stromal remodeling, and predicted immunotherapy response, but its prognostic effect varies between models and discrimination improvement is small.

papers.abstract: Background In recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (R/M HNSCC), early identification of treatment response remains challenging because imaging may be delayed or confounded by treatment-related changes and atypical response patterns under immunotherapy. Serial circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analysis may provide a minimally invasive measure of tumor dynamics and complement conventional imaging. We therefore investigated the feasibility and clinical relevance of patient-specific droplet digital PCR (ddPCR)-based ctDNA monitoring. Methods Nine patients with R/M HNSCC underwent tumor genomic profiling using FoundationOne ® CDx as part of routine clinical care. Patient-specific single-nucleotide variants, including pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and technically suitable variants of uncertain significance, were selected for ddPCR assay development. Plasma samples were collected before and/or during systemic treatment, and ctDNA kinetics were assessed in relation to radiologic response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Results Sixteen single-target ddPCR assays were successfully established and combined into ten patient-specific single- or multi-target assay configurations. A total of 21 plasma samples were analyzed, and technically valid measurements were obtained for all samples. Pretreatment plasma was available for seven patients, of whom three (42.9%) had detectable ctDNA. Across all time points, ctDNA was detected at least once in six of nine patients (66.7%). Among the six patients with serial sampling, ctDNA kinetics showed descriptive agreement with radiologic assessment in five (83.3%). The single patient with increasing ctDNA developed progressive disease, whereas decreasing or stable ctDNA was accompanied by partial response or stable disease in four patients; one patient showed a mixed radiologic response. In an exploratory descriptive comparison, the single patient with increasing ctDNA had shorter observed PFS and OS than the five patients with decreasing or stable ctDNA levels. Given the group size of one patient, this observation is hypothesis-generating and does not establish a prognostic association. Conclusions Patient-specific ddPCR-based ctDNA monitoring was technically feasible and showed agreement with radiologic assessment in most evaluable patients. These proof-of-concept findings support prospective evaluation of patient-specific ddPCR as a focused approach for longitudinal monitoring in R/M HNSCC; its comparative clinical utility and cost-effectiveness remain to be established.

papers.abstract: Hepatoid adenocarcinoma (HAC) is a rare extrahepatic adenocarcinoma producing alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), with clinicopathological features resembling hepatocellular carcinoma, including aggressive behavior, poor prognosis, vascular invasion, and distant metastasis. It occurs mostly in the stomach and rarely in the colon. Due to its rarity, large randomized trials are lacking; thus, case reports provide valuable treatment information. Here, we report a 62-year-old woman initially diagnosed with massive hepatocellular carcinoma by computed tomography (CT) who underwent radical hepatectomy. Postoperative follow-up CT revealed lesions in the sigmoid colon and residual liver. Colonoscopic biopsy showed poorly differentiated carcinoma (adenocarcinoma with enteroblastic differentiation/hepatoid adenocarcinoma). She then received CAPOX (oxaliplatin plus capecitabine) combined with sintilimab and bevacizumab. After one year, follow-up imaging showed complete disappearance of the liver tumor and reduction of the sigmoid colon lesion. The final efficacy assessment was complete remission (CR) of the liver lesion and stable disease (SD) of the sigmoid colon lesion. This case report suggests that combined immune-targeted therapy and chemotherapy achieved excellent efficacy in a patient with intestinal hepatoid adenocarcinoma and liver metastases, and this combination regimen may provide a new treatment strategy for intestinal hepatoid adenocarcinoma (IHA).

papers.abstract: Background SLC25A28 encodes the mitochondrial iron transporter mitoferrin-2, but its prognostic relevance and biological associations in glioma remain incompletely characterized. We investigated its clinical significance and relationships with metabolic, ferroptosis-related and immune features across glioma cohorts. Methods SLC25-family genes were screened in CGGA and TCGA, followed by survival analysis and meta-analysis across nine GlioVis cohorts. Clinical Cox models, prognostic scores and grade/IDH subgroups were evaluated. Metabolic, immune and curated ferroptosis-related signatures were examined using clinically adjusted models, and immune-cell and checkpoint analyses underwent false-discovery-rate correction. SLC25A28 expression was assessed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting. Results Lower SLC25A28 expression was associated with unfavorable clinicopathological features and shorter overall survival (pooled hazard ratio, 1.91; 95% confidence interval, 1.46–2.50; I² = 84.9%). Exploratory analyses supported survival associations in both IDH-mutant and IDH-wild-type subgroups of CGGA and TCGA, although findings within glioblastoma varied. Positive oxidative-phosphorylation associations persisted after grade/IDH adjustment in both pooled cohorts; within glioblastoma, this association was supported in CGGA but not TCGA. Ferroptosis-related transcriptional associations were also detected, with consistent all-glioma WikiPathways results across sensitivity analyses in TCGA but scoring-method and cohort dependence in regulator signatures. Immune-cell differences survived correction for 10 of 22 populations in CGGA and 16 of 22 in TCGA, and three checkpoint genes showed positive correlations in both cohorts. qRT-PCR and Western blotting confirmed lower SLC25A28 expression in U87 and U251 cells than in normal human astrocytes. Conclusions SLC25A28 is a candidate prognostic biomarker associated with mitochondrial metabolism, ferroptosis-related transcriptional features and immune features in glioma. Multi-cohort survival evidence and clinically adjusted molecular associations support further evaluation of its prognostic and biological relevance. Subtype-specific clinical validation and functional investigations will help define its clinical utility and biological role.

papers.abstract: Early diagnosis of ovarian cancer is a significant clinical problem, and this is mainly because there are no strongly sensitive early-detection biomarkers, and the standard screening parameters like CA-125 blood tests and transvaginal ultrasounds are very insensitive in making a diagnosis. This paper presents a machine learning architecture, which is organized and interpretable based on the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening data to enhance the risk stratification of ovarian cancer. The original analytical cohort comprised 78,209 participants, including 518 ovarian cancer cases. To select 20 informative pre-diagnostic predictors in a high dimensional feature space, a comprehensive feature selection pipeline with ANOVA (f classifier), Chi-square, Random Forest importance, and XGBoost importance were used. Several classification algorithms were tested and the boosting based methods proved to have a good predictive value. A stacking ensemble of K-Nearest Neighbors and AdaBoost was the highest performing overall (accuracy: 0.7644), and a test-set AUROC of 0.8399, with additional evaluation using sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, balanced accuracy, MCC, and PR-AUC. SHAP analysis and permutation importance were used to provide model interpretability and consistently regarded questionnaire-based screening variables, age, and CA-125 attributes as the strongest ones. The suggested framework offers a methodologically rigorous and transparent method of assessment of population level ovarian cancer risk, providing a foundation for future research toward a clinically useful ovarian cancer screening decision-support system, pending external validation.

papers.abstract: Background Accurate differentiation between benign and malignant spinal tumors is critical for treatment planning, yet manual interpretation of T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI remains subjective, with substantial inter-observer variability. This study aimed to develop a deep learning model, the multi-scale deep residual network (MSDR-Net), for automated benign–malignant classification. Methods A total of 500 T2-weighted fat-suppressed MR images of pathologically confirmed spinal tumors (389 benign, 111 malignant) were retrospectively collected from two institutions. Data were partitioned into training (70%), validation (20%), and independent test (10%) sets, and five-fold cross-validation was performed. Leave-one-center-out external validation was also performed (development: Institution A, n = 300; evaluation: Institution B, n = 200). The proposed MSDR-Net incorporates multi-branch residual blocks that combine parallel multi-scale convolutional paths with efficient channel attention modules and was benchmarked against six established architectures. Results On the independent test set (N = 50; 12 malignant cases), MSDR-Net achieved 92.0% accuracy, 91.7% sensitivity (95% CI 61.5%–99.8%), 92.1% specificity, and an AUC of 0.921, the highest point estimates among evaluated architectures. The model was well calibrated (Brier score 0.072), with net benefit over treat-all strategies across thresholds of 0.10–0.60. Derived from a small test cohort, these estimates carry substantial uncertainty and await confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts. External-cohort accuracy was 86.5% (AUC 0.875). Ablation experiments showed that removing either component degraded performance, with a modest super-additive interaction; given their substantially smaller capacity, the single-path variants’ deficit cannot be attributed solely to removing multi-scale processing. The model has 55.4M parameters and 12.3-ms inference per image. Conclusion MSDR-Net effectively captures multi-scale discriminative features of spinal tumors on T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI, achieving high classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. The model shows promise for clinical deployment as an auxiliary diagnostic tool for orthopedic surgeons and radiologists.

papers.abstract: Objective To comprehensively assess the association of pretreatment systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) with the prognosis of gastric cancer patients. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched to select studies exploring the association of SII with the overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS) or recurrence-free survival (RFS) of gastric cancer. We pooled the hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a random-effects model. Robustness was assessed by sensitivity analyses, and publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test. Results A total of 61 studies involving 66 cohorts and 31,608 patients were included in this meta-analysis, with most studies adopting a retrospective design and only one prospective study enrolled. Elevated pretreatment SII was significantly correlated with inferior OS (HR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.36–1.62), PFS (HR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.30–1.58), and RFS (HR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.09–1.76). Subgroup analyses demonstrated that the magnitude of the prognostic association varied across treatment modalities and geographic regions. Conclusion In conclusion, we found that elevated pretreatment SII is a potential biomarker for adverse prognosis in gastric cancer patients. However, since nearly all included studies were retrospective and only one was a prospective study, our findings support the prognostic value of SII, but prospective validation is required before routine clinical implementation. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/ , identifier CRD420261321880.

papers.abstract: Introduction To develop and validate a multimodal CT-based model integrating intra-peritumoral radiomics, 2.5D deep learning (DL), and clinical-radiological features for preoperative prediction of World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grade in older patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Methods This multicenter retrospective study included 1,103 patients older than 60 years with pathologically confirmed ccRCC from four hospitals. Patients were allocated to a training cohort (n=459), an internal validation cohort (n=198), and two independent external test cohorts (test1, n=227; test2, n=219). WHO/ISUP grades I–II were classified as low grade and grades III–IV as high grade. Radiomics features were extracted from corticomedullary-phase CT images using intratumoral and progressively expanded intra-peritumoral regions of 1, 2, and 3 mm. In parallel, 2D and 2.5D DL features were extracted using ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 networks, with the 2.5D approach integrating axial, coronal, and sagittal tumor views. After feature selection, five machine learning classifiers were evaluated. The optimal radiomics model, DL model, and clinical model were integrated using stacking-based decision-level fusion. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results The random forest (RF) model based on intra-peritumoral 3-mm radiomics features achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.754 (95% CI, 0.683–0.825) and 0.725 (95% CI, 0.655–0.794) in the test1 and test2 cohorts, respectively. The RF model based on 2.5D DL features achieved corresponding AUCs of 0.756 (95% CI, 0.682–0.830) and 0.713 (95% CI, 0.643–0.783). The multimodal combined model achieved numerically higher external AUCs than the selected single-modality models, reaching 0.775 (95% CI, 0.705–0.845) in test1 and 0.732 (95% CI, 0.664–0.800) in test2. DCA demonstrated favorable clinical net benefit for the combined model, while SHAP analysis identified the 2.5D DL component as the largest contributor to model predictions. Discussion A multimodal CT-based framework integrating intra-peritumoral radiomics, 2.5D DL, and clinical-radiological information enabled noninvasive preoperative prediction of WHO/ISUP grade in older patients with ccRCC and maintained predictive performance across independent external cohorts. This approach may provide complementary imaging and clinical information for preoperative risk stratification and individualized treatment planning.

papers.abstract: Background Sarcopenia and osteoporosis are linked to poor treatment outcomes and are significantly underdiagnosed in esophageal cancer patients. Despite the promising efficacy of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NACI) in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), predicting treatment response remains a major clinical hurdle. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the associations of sarcopenia and osteoporosis on pathological response and to develop a both clinical and computed tomography (CT)-based predictive model for NACI outcomes in ESCC patients. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted in 179 patients with ESCC who underwent radical resection after neoadjuvant tislelizumab, albumin-bound paclitaxel, and nedaplatin. Within each of 500 stratified bootstrap resamples, five-fold cross-validation was used to determine the optimal LASSO penalty parameter, followed by Firth logistic regression. Aggregated out-of-bag predictions underwent five-fold cross-fitted recalibration. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were evaluated using the AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, Brier score, calibration intercept and slope, Hosmer–Lemeshow test, and decision curve analysis. Results Major pathological response (MPR) rates were 70.0%, 40.0%, 22.0%, and 8.3% in the control, osteoporosis-only, sarcopenia-only, and osteosarcopenia groups, respectively. In multivariable Firth logistic regression, lower tumor grading, absence of comorbidities, absence of lymphovascular invasion, absence of sarcopenia, and a higher intermuscular adipose tissue (IMAT) area percentage were associated with a greater likelihood of achieving MPR, whereas osteoporosis was not associated with MPR (P = 0.130). The cross-fitted recalibrated model achieved an AUC of 0.885 (95% CI, 0.835–0.934), with 0.818 accuracy, 0.840 sensitivity, and 0.800 specificity at a threshold of 0.405. Calibration was satisfactory (Brier score, 0.136; intercept, −0.009; slope, 0.960; Hosmer–Lemeshow P = 0.219), and decision curve analysis showed clinical net benefit across thresholds of 0.08–0.80. Conclusion Absence of sarcopenia and a higher IMAT area percentage were associated with a greater likelihood of achieving major pathological response. The combined clinical and CT-based model showed good internally validated performance.

papers.abstract: Background Sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma (sRCC) is a rare and aggressive subtype of renal cell carcinoma with a poor prognosis. Accurate prognostic stratification is critical for individualized treatment planning. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning-based prognostic model integrating multiphase CT radiomics and clinicopathological factors to predict overall survival (OS) in patients with pathology-confirmed sRCC. Methods A total of 113 patients with pathologically confirmed sRCC who underwent nephrectomy were retrospectively enrolled. Radiomic features were extracted from arterial phase (AP) and venous phase (VP) CT images. After feature selection using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC > 0.75) and univariate Cox regression, a radiomics signature was constructed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression and random survival forest (RSF) algorithms. A combined model was developed by integrating the radiomics score with independent clinical predictors identified through multivariate Cox regression. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling and repeated cross-validation. Results The combined model, incorporating the AP+VP radiomics score, N stage, M stage, and Ki-67 index, showed numerically improved predictive performance compared with the clinical model. In the held-out test set, it achieved a C-index of 0.737 (95% CI: 0.612–0.846), which was comparable to the AP+VP radiomics model alone (C-index: 0.735) and numerically higher than the clinical model (C-index: 0.615); however, the improvement over the clinical model was not statistically significant (P = 0.115). AUCs for 1-, 2-, and 3-year OS were 0.833, 0.780, and 0.749, respectively. The model showed good calibration and clinical utility across a range of threshold probabilities. Significant survival stratification was achieved between high- and low-risk groups (log-rank P < 0.05). Conclusions The proposed machine learning model combining multiphase CT radiomics and clinicopathological factors may provide a noninvasive tool for predicting OS in sRCC patients. It showed numerically improved performance compared with conventional clinical models; however, this incremental benefit was not statistically significant, and its performance was comparable to the radiomics-only model. Further multicenter validation is warranted to confirm its generalizability.

papers.abstract: Introduction Macrophages in the tumor microenvironment are known to upregulate PD-L1 expression, thereby suppressing T cells through PD-1 ligation. However, the manner in which PD-L1 expression intrinsically impacts macrophages and their immunomodulatory phenotype is less clear. Clarifying this knowledge gap may provide further insight into macrophage function within the tumor microenvironment. Methods To characterize the macrophage intrinsic role of PD-L1, we used complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches by analyzing primary murine bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) with complete genetic PDL1 deletion and wildtype BMDMs treated with anti-PD-L1 blocking antibodies. Macrophages were evaluated in vitro across naïve, pro-inflammatory, and tumor conditioned polarization states. Results Unlike prior reports, neither genetic deletion nor antibody blockade dramatically altered the expression of macrophage polarization markers or in vitro phagocytic capacity. However, both conditions consistently and robustly reduced surface levels of a costimulatory molecule, CD80. Reduced CD80 levels prompted further analysis of T cell interacting and antigen presentation associated surface proteins, in which we revealed disparate effects of expression in response to PD-L1 genetic deletion and antibody blockade. Discussion Collectively, these findings suggest that loss of macrophage PD-L1 reduces CD80 expression and regulates immunoregulatory surface protein expression in vitro .

papers.abstract: Cell competition is a conserved fitness-surveillance process, first described in Drosophila epithelia, by which cells compare relative fitness with their neighbors so that less-fit “loser” cells are eliminated, extruded or forced to differentiate while fitter “winner” cells expand. In the tumor microenvironment (TME), this logic appears to be co-opted by transformed clones that eliminate normal epithelium, outcompete neighboring subclones and reshape stromal and immune compartments, making cell competition a potentially underappreciated contributor to cancer clonal evolution, immune escape and therapy resistance. Because competition is defined by a comparison between adjacent cells and by a demonstrated change in the relative representation of one population, it is difficult to resolve with bulk sequencing, which averages across precisely the heterogeneity that defines it. The convergence of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics, spatial and single-cell proteomics, artificial intelligence (AI) and network-inference bioinformatics now allows competition-relevant cellular states, interfaces and signaling relationships to be measured at the resolution the problem requires. We emphasize at the outset that these technologies are, in almost all current applications, hypothesis-generating: they identify candidate competitive interfaces and putative winner and loser states from static measurements, and they do not by themselves demonstrate that competition has occurred. This review synthesizes advances across these domains; proposes an explicit three-tier evidence framework separating direct experimental evidence of cell competition from competition-relevant associations and from computational predictions; distinguishes cell competition from related processes such as clonal selection, immune editing and differential proliferation; and defines a putative cell competition network as a falsifiable construct whose edges include ligand-receptor, spatial-adjacency, metabolic and mechanical relations. We further outline a conceptual, context-dependent Cell Competition Score (CCS) as a testable specification rather than a biomarker-ready instrument, and set out the benchmarking, causal-inference and prospective-validation requirements that stand between current capability and any clinical application.

papers.abstract: Background Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) progression is closely linked to a complex tumor microenvironment (TME), yet key regulators remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically investigate the roles of TMC8 in ccRCC, focusing on its immunological and biological potential. Methods Multi-cohort transcriptomic data were integrated to analyze TMC8 expression and prognostic value. Functional enrichment and multiple immune deconvolution algorithms were applied to characterize TME associations. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis characterized TMC8 -associated transcriptional features across immune-cell populations. Sex-stratified analyses were performed to identify dimorphic effects. In vitro and in vivo experiments were conducted to validate the biological functions of TMC8 . Results TMC8 was significantly upregulated in ccRCC and associated with poor overall survival, particularly in males. Its expression correlated with higher estimated immune infiltration and antigen-presentation-related signatures, alongside elevated expression of exhaustion-associated markers. scRNA-seq analysis suggested the uncoupling of T-cell activation and effector competence. Notably, TMC8 exhibited marked sex-specific associations, with stronger oncogenic and immunological associations in males. Functionally, TMC8 promoted tumor progression by enhancing proliferation, migration, and invasion, which were suppressed upon TMC8 knockdown in vitro and in vivo . Conclusion TMC8 is associated with dysregulated oncogenic signaling and an immunologically active yet dysfunctional TME in ccRCC, with pronounced sex-specific associations, and may represent a putative therapeutic target warranting further validation.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ocular involvement in primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) can be difficult to identify, highlighting the need for noninvasive biomarkers that may support its detection. We investigated optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) biomarkers associated with ocular involvement in PCNSL. This retrospective single‐center study included 62 eyes from 36 patients with PCNSL after exclusion of confounding vitreoretinal disease and poor‐quality OCTA scans. Eyes were classified as having ocular involvement (OI; n = 23) or no ocular involvement (NOI; n = 39), and follow‐up OCTA was available for 23 eyes from 14 patients. Macular and optic‐disc OCTA parameters were analyzed, and discriminatory performance was assessed using direction‐corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). OI eyes showed predominantly deep capillary plexus (DCP)‐specific reductions in macular perfusion. DCP whole‐image inferior hemifield perfusion density was lower in OI than NOI eyes (44.95 ± 6.01% vs. 51.06 ± 6.11%; p < 0.001; AUC, 0.776), as was DCP whole‐image perfusion density (45.92 ± 6.12% vs. 51.98 ± 6.13%; p < 0.001; AUC, 0.764). In the follow‐up subset, the corresponding AUCs were 0.947 and 0.932. Neither metric showed significant within‐group changes over time, and longitudinal analyses revealed no consistent treatment‐associated perfusion pattern. These findings identify a predominantly DCP‐specific macular microvascular phenotype associated with ocular involvement in PCNSL and support DCP perfusion metrics as candidate noninvasive imaging biomarkers that may complement clinical assessment and intraocular fluid‐based evaluation.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Antibodies against HPV proteins can provide pre‐diagnostic information about cancer development. We described the prevalence of antibodies to proteins of oncogenic HPV types prior to diagnosis of HPV‐related cancers. We analysed pre‐diagnostic blood from 1700 participants with incident HPV‐related cancers (anal = 387, cervical = 274, oropharyngeal = 788, penile = 168, vaginal = 83) and 6221 controls from nine prospective cohorts in Europe, North America and Australia in the HPV Cancer Cohort Consortium. We measured antibodies against E6, E7 and L1 proteins for 6 HPV types, and additionally against E1, E2, E4, E6, E7 and L1 proteins of HPV16 and 18. We described seroprevalence by lead time from blood draw to cancer diagnosis (range: 0–43 years). We found that among oropharyngeal cancers, seroprevalence increased approaching diagnosis for HPV16 E1, E2, E4, E6, E7, L1 and HPV18 E1, E2, L1 (HPV16‐E6: from 10.4% at > 20 years to 35.8% at 0–5 years, vs. 0.3% in controls). Anal cancer showed similar patterns for HPV16 E1, E2, E4, E6 and L1 and HPV18 E2 (HPV16‐E6: from 3.8% at > 20 years to 29.8% at 0–5 years). No trends were observed for cervical, penile, or vaginal cancers. In a multivariable model fit among cases, HPV16‐E6 seropositivity was higher at shorter lead times and more recent calendar periods, lower among US non‐Hispanic Blacks, and varied by cancer type (highest in oropharyngeal followed by anal, vaginal, penile and cervical) (all p < 0.03). In conclusion, pre‐diagnostic HPV antibody responses vary by cancer type, with seroprevalence of 6–9 HPV proteins increasing approaching diagnosis for oropharyngeal and anal cancers, but not cervical, penile or vaginal cancers.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is usually detected with mammography screening and assumed to be a precursor of invasive ductal cancer (IDC) of the breast. Yet, despite an approximately 10‐fold increase in the rate of DCIS detection and treatment within 20 years following implementation of mammography screening in the United States, IDC incidence rates remained comparatively stable (a 1.6‐fold increase during the same time period). Moreover, if we accept the assumption that DCIS is a nonobligate precursor of IDC, with estimates that up to 40% may progress to IDC, then DCIS annual incidence should be at least 2.5‐fold greater than that of IDC, and at least 9‐fold greater than what is now reported. Such a vast underestimation of DCIS incidence seems unlikely, as over 85% of all DCIS lesions contain microcalcifications and most should therefore be detectable with modern breast screening technology. In this special report, we discuss evidence derived from population‐based registries suggesting that DCIS is not a precursor but rather a low‐risk variant of invasive breast cancer, with a 3.3% risk of breast cancer death over a 20‐year period. A large DCIS treatment trial with a mortality endpoint is needed to bolster support for this alternative hypothesis and potentially justify treating DCIS as a low‐risk systemic disease.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Timely diagnosis and risk stratification of endometrial cancer (EC) remain difficult in resource‐limited regions. This prospective diagnostic accuracy and feasibility study evaluated whether self‐collected cervical specimens combined with CDO1/CELF4 methylation testing, defined as the CISENDO assay, could identify histologically confirmed EC in symptomatic women from Gansu, northwest China. Of 302 screened women, 154 participants with self‐collected specimens and histopathological diagnoses formed the primary analytic cohort; 35 had EC and 119 had non‐EC diagnoses. An exploratory paired subset included 35 participants with both self‐ and physician‐collected specimens. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis and logistic regression, while paired sampling was evaluated using correlation, Bland–Altman analysis, and classification concordance. In self‐collected specimens, CISENDO showed strong discrimination for EC at manufacturer‐defined cutoffs (AUC 0.834). Bland–Altman mean differences were −1.05 ΔCt for CDO1 and −1.73 ΔCt for CELF4. CISENDO classifications were concordant in 31/35 paired specimens (88.6%), with positive agreement of 84.6%, negative agreement of 90.9%, and Cohen's κ of 0.76. CISENDO positivity remained the strongest independent predictor of EC after adjustment (adjusted OR 85.08; 95% CI 12.21–592.71; p < 0.001). Endometrial thickness showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.646) and did not improve performance when combined with CISENDO. Self‐collected CISENDO testing showed strong discrimination for histologically confirmed EC and may provide a feasible molecular triage and risk‐stratification approach for symptomatic women in underserved settings. This approach could support decentralized sample collection and reduce dependence on immediate specialist‐based evaluation, particularly in geographically dispersed, resource‐constrained populations.

papers.abstract: LUAD exhibits diversity in the mechanisms of angiogenesis and the tumor environment's responses to anti-VEGF therapy, while the tumor-cell-intrinsic mechanisms that prevent vascularization are not well understood. SCGB3A2 (secretoglobin 3A2; HIN-2/UGRP1) is a club/secretory marker of pulmonary adenocarcinoma without established angiogenic function. By using an unsupervised integration approach of two public LUAD single-cell RNA-seq cohorts, we described a SCGB3A2-high malignant epithelial state characterized by an angiogenesis-low phenotype as indicated by the low presence of VEGFA, hypoxic conditions, and a low epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), along with a secretory/anti-inflammatory program, which was confirmed in independent bulk cohorts (TCGA-LUAD, GSE72094) showing that SCGB3A2-high tumors experienced lower instances of angiogenesis, hypoxia, and scores related to EMT/invasion. Using spatial transcriptomics, we positioned SCGB3A2-high tumor cells next to endothelial cells and identified a spatially inferred VEGFA/B-FLT1 interaction pattern. In A549 and NCI-H1975 cells, conditioned medium from SCGB3A2-overexpressing cells contained higher levels of extracellular PGK2-immunoreactive signal and angiostatin and was associated with reduced HUVEC tube formation and VEGFR2 phosphorylation. Thus, SCGB3A2 is a marker for LUAD tumors characterized by low levels of angiogenesis, which is associated with an extracellular PGK2/angiostatin signal.

papers.abstract: The excellent cure rates achieved in testicular cancer represent one of oncology's major success stories. Decades of research have optimized survival, leading to cure for nearly all patients with localized disease and most with metastatic disease. As a result, attention is increasingly shifting from survival alone to reducing treatment burden and long-term toxicity while improving quality of life in this predominantly young population with decades-long life expectancy. However, many adolescent and young adult survivors experience persistent physical, psychological, and social consequences that are insufficiently addressed by conventional follow-up care. Current survivorship models remain largely centered on relapse surveillance and provide limited education or support for understanding late effects, managing uncertainty, or developing long-term self-management skills. Limited empowerment may undermine sustained engagement with follow-up care and long-term well-being. This article makes the case for a shift from hospital-centered information delivery models toward more engaging, experiential, patient-centered survivorship frameworks. We propose extended reality-based immersive and interactive digital technologies as enabling tools within a broader survivorship framework designed to support understanding, early symptom recognition, engagement, and shared decision-making beyond scheduled hospital visits. Using the TRANSCEND-XR consortium as an illustrative example, we discuss how co-designed digital interventions may help bridge the gap between cure and long-term quality of life while addressing key clinical, ethical, and implementation challenges relevant to scalability. PATIENT SUMMARY: Many young people cured of testicular cancer experience long-term physical and emotional challenges that are not fully addressed by routine follow-up care. We describe a new approach using extended reality technologies to help survivors better understand late effects, recognize symptoms early, and take a more active role in their care. Such approaches aim to improve quality of life, support long-term well-being, and facilitate a successful transition from cancer treatment to life beyond cancer. papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose: We report the long-term survival outcomes of a modified-intensity lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (RVD-lite) regimen as a first-line treatment for transplant-ineligible multiple myeloma. Patients and Methods: RVD-lite was evaluated in an investigator-initiated, multicenter phase II trial in patients with transplant-ineligible multiple myeloma. RVD-lite was administered over a 35-day cycle with lenalidomide 15 mg orally on days 1 to 21; bortezomib 1.3 mg/m2 subcutaneously on days 1, 8, 15, and 22; and dexamethasone 20 mg orally on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15, 16, 22, and 23 in patients ≤75 years of age and on days 1, 8, 15, and 22 in patients >75 years of age for 9 cycles of induction followed by 6 cycles of consolidation (lenalidomide + bortezomib). Lenalidomide maintenance was not mandated. Results: Fifty patients were enrolled. The median age was 73 years (range, 65–91), and 14% of patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 2. At best response, the overall response rate (ORR) and ≥ very good partial response (VGPR) were 90% and 66%, respectively. After a median follow-up of 72 months, the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 42 months (5-year PFS: 40%), and the median overall survival (OS) was 76 months (5-year OS: 63%). An ECOG performance status of 2 was associated with inferior PFS and OS. Thirty-three (66%) patients received lenalidomide maintenance. Two (4%) patients discontinued treatment because of toxicity, and there was no treatment-related mortality. Conclusions: RVD-lite is a well-tolerated and highly effective regimen in transplant-ineligible multiple myeloma with prolonged PFS and OS. This study provides the framework for frailty-adapted triplet and quadruplet regimens in patients with multiple myeloma. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01782963).

papers.abstract: Abstract Li–Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is caused by germline likely pathogenic/pathogenic variants in the TP53 gene which encodes the p53 tumor suppressor. LFS is a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS) with significant lifelong multiorgan cancer risk. As one of the earliest described and less common CPS, knowledge of LFS has grown significantly over time through international collaboration. Future progress in the management of these patients is dependent upon clinical and research advances as facilitated by disease-specific patient/family meetings like the LFS Association bi-annual REACH meeting. This meeting brings together scientists, clinicians, and patients with LFS and their family members in a collaborative effort to explore challenges in the field. Major current areas of study in LFS include (i) improving our understanding of specific p53 tumor suppressive functions necessary for cancer development, (ii) developing novel classification systems for TP53 variants, (iii) exploring more precise genotype–phenotype correlations, (iv) defining the cancer spectrum to better inform risk prediction for patients, and (v) understanding the psychosocial implications of an LFS diagnosis. Areas of need were also identified, particularly the need for more precise and practical methods of cancer screening and innovative strategies for targeting the p53 pathway for cancer prevention or early tumor interception. This commentary reflects the major advances in understanding of LFS, including most up-to-date research in the field related to p53 biology, variant interpretation, and clinical care. Herein, we also review areas of late-breaking research and future directions in the field, as a “call to action” for LFS researchers and clinicians.

papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose: All targeted therapies approved for ROS1 fusion–positive non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) are type I inhibitors. These tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) may induce resistance amenable to type II inhibition. Cabozantinib is a type II ROS1/MET TKI with preclinical activity against on-target ROS1 resistance mutations and MET alterations. Patients and Methods: This single-center, open-label, phase II study (NCT01639508) enrolled patients with pretreated ROS1 fusion–positive NSCLC. The primary endpoint was the objective response rate (ORR). Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety. The first phase of the Simon two-stage design is reported. Results: Seven ROS1 TKI pretreated patients were enrolled. Previous treatment included crizotinib, entrectinib, repotrectinib, and zidesamtinib. The ORR was 43% [95% confidence interval (CI), 10%–81.5%]. The best response was −92% partial response (PR) in a patient with ROS1 D2033N–mutant cancer. Two additional PRs were achieved, one (−49%) in an ROS1 G2032R/L2086F–mutant cancer. The median PFS was 4.5 months [95% CI, 4–not estimable (NE)] with a median duration of response and OS of 8 (95% CI, 3–13) and 11 months (95% CI, 6–NE), respectively. Resistance mechanisms to cabozantinib were identified in two patients: MET overexpression and MET D1228N. The most frequent treatment-related toxicities observed were fatigue, nausea, and hypertension. Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 57%, mostly palmar–plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPE) and transaminitis. All patients required a dose reduction. Conclusions: Cabozantinib achieved responses in pretreated ROS1 fusion–positive NSCLCs, even in the presence of multidrug-resistant mutations, highlighting the potential utility of type II ROS1 TKI therapy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose: CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) are being investigated in endometrial cancer clinical trials, with some patients showing a significant response. However, there are few biomarkers to predict which endometrial cancer patients will respond to CDK4/6is. Current inclusion criteria include endometrial cancer histology and/or lack of certain genetic alterations. We hypothesize that instead, endometrial cancer patients should be included or excluded from CDK4/6i clinical trials based on the retinoblastoma protein (RB)-functional status of the tumor, defined by the activity of RB function–predictive transcriptional signatures. Experimental Design: We analyzed RB1 and TP53 mutation status, RB protein expression, baseline transcriptional profiles, and RB function-predictive transcriptional signatures in endometrial cancer samples from 39 patients who participated in two combination clinical trials of the CDK4/6i abemaciclib, one testing letrozole/abemaciclib and the other letrozole/metformin/abemaciclib (NCT03675893). All patients had estrogen receptor–positive endometrial cancers of varying molecular subtypes, with the majority of cases being of endometrioid histology. We statistically assessed for correlation of the results of these analyses with objective response to the CDK4/6i in the clinical trials. Results: We show that RB protein expression levels and RB1 mutation status do not correlate with CDK4/6i response. Rather, we show that decreased activity of multiple RB function–predictive transcriptional signatures, which suggests that RB is functional, corresponds to response to the CDK4/6i. We show that reduced expression of specific E2F family members correlates with CDK4/6i response. Conclusions: These results suggest that RB function–predictive transcriptional signatures may be a relevant biomarker for CDK4/6i response in endometrial cancer and merit further refinement and validation in the clinical setting.
