papers.abstract: Purpose Patients with hematologic cancer rate fatigue as their most frequent and severe unmet issue. Methylphenidate (MTP) has been reported to alleviate cancer-related fatigue (CRF) in some studies, but data from hematologic cancers are lacking. We investigated MTP for hematologic CRF. Methods Using a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, two-period, crossover design, 152 adult fatigued patients with hematologic cancer were randomly assigned to 6 weeks of either MTP or placebo, with a treatment-free week before the crossover. Eligibility required a Visual Analog Scale fatigue score ≥4 (range, 0-10), hemoglobin ≥8.0 g/dL, no chemotherapy within 8 weeks, and no concomitant psychopharmacologic treatment. The primary end point was the between-group difference in the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy–Fatigue (FACIT-F) score from baseline to end of each period. Results The median age was 59.0 years (range, 21-83), 44% were women, the performance status was 0 in 57.3%, and 11% had received high-dose therapy. FACIT-F improved 8.9 points (95% CIs, 7.3 to 10.4) after MTP and 3.9 points (95% CI, 2.3 to 5.4) after placebo. The between-group difference of 5.0 points (95% CI, 2.8 to 7.2) was in favor of MTP. Reduced fatigue ratings in favor of MTP were also observed using other tools. Toxicity was mild, but more adverse events were reported during the MTP (N = 73; 57%) versus placebo (N = 52; 40%) periods. Conclusion MTP treatment alleviated fatigue and may be considered as a pharmacologic fatigue intervention in patients with hematologic cancer.

papers.abstract: Platelet RNA profiling is a promising liquid biopsy approach, offering minimally invasive insights into systemic diseases, such as cancer. Yet, the effect of leukocyte-associated RNA retention on platelet transcriptomic signatures remains unclear. This study provides the first comprehensive evaluation of how leukocyte-associated RNA retention influences platelet RNA sequencing and machine learning (ML)-based cancer detection. Using the largest publicly available platelet transcriptomic dataset (2351 human RNA samples) and single-cell/single-platelet RNA sequencing from 29 donors, we quantified leukocyte-associated RNA retention in matched sample groups (low vs. high retention) via a novel 132-gene leukocyte marker panel. Diagnostic implications were assessed using 10 ML algorithms for binary classification (cancer vs. healthy), examining the contribution of leukocyte-derived transcripts. Interestingly, models trained on high-retention samples often showed slightly improved performance, suggesting complementary diagnostic value from leukocyte signals. Importantly, post hoc correction using remove unwanted variation (RUV) and linear modeling effectively mitigated retention effects. However, adding the leukocyte-associated RNA retention score to the full-cohort classifier changed cancer-detection AUC only minimally (0.9247 to 0.9249). Thus, whether this signal should be corrected, recalibrated, or reported should depend on the study question rather than assuming routine removal.

papers.abstract: High-risk patients need to carefully consider the risks and benefits of surgery. Shared decision-making is a collaborative process that enables patients and clinicians to share information and weigh up options and preferences. There is limited evidence about how best to organise the participation of the full range of healthcare professionals who can contribute to such decision-making processes. We conducted a Delphi study with a panel of experts to clarify how, and for what purposes, different healthcare professionals can contribute to shared decision-making with high-risk surgical patients. Consensus was reached on a conceptual model of multidisciplinary shared decision-making. The model recommends that interactions between patients, supported by family members and informal carers, and healthcare professionals are organised around five areas: options for management and treatment; patient values, goals, and preferences; comprehensive needs assessment; social context and home environment; and perioperative preparations. Experts agreed that achieving multidisciplinary shared decision-making in practice requires four key facilitators: early identification of patients with complex decision-making needs, availability of specialist expertise and support, sufficient time for discussion and decision-making, and coordination and information sharing between interactions. This model organises multidisciplinary involvement in high-risk surgical shared decision-making into five conceptually distinct and operationally interdependent areas. The model has the potential to inform practice and enhance opportunities for shared decision-making for high-risk surgical patients and their multidisciplinary teams.

papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a near-universally lethal malignancy, with KRAS mutations driving tumorigenesis in over 90% of cases. For decades considered undruggable, oncogenic KRAS has now been therapeutically engaged across multiple mutational subtypes, a revolution precipitated by allele-specific covalent inhibitors and accelerated by the emergence of RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitors. The pivotal phase 3 RASolute 302 trial of daraxonrasib, a pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor, demonstrated nearly doubled median overall survival (13.2 versus 6.7 months; HR 0.40; P < 0.0001) over standard chemotherapy in previously treated metastatic PDAC. Concurrently, mutation-selective G12D inhibitors (zoldonrasib, VS-7375, INCB161734), G12D-targeted protein degraders (setidegrasib), G12C-selective RAS(ON) compounds (elironrasib), and next-generation MEK inhibitors (atebimetinib) are advancing through clinical evaluation. This review synthesizes the biological basis of KRAS-driven oncogenesis in the pancreas, the mutational landscape and its prognostic implications, the structural and mechanistic evolution of KRAS inhibitor classes, contemporary and emerging clinical data from recent trials, toxicity profiles and their management, and resistance mechanisms. The field stands at an inflection point: daraxonrasib now redefines second-line PDAC management, while first-line combination regimens with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy have produced an ORR of 58% in early-phase single-arm data, a result now being tested in the randomized RASolute 303 trial. The challenge ahead lies in translating these results into durable remissions through rational combination therapy and in overcoming acquired resistance.

papers.abstract: With the emergence of radiotheranostics, radiation oncology practices are adapting to offer new radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs), while qualified medical physicists (QMPs) support these programs. However, RPT-specific medical physics training is variable, and heavily dependent on the clinical setting. QMPs may therefore be tasked with supporting RPT programs without adequate training in the subject matter. In 2025, the Nuclear Oncology Division of the Department of Radiation Oncology at Willis Knighton Cancer Center launched a first-of-kind, one-year Nuclear Oncology Physics Fellowship. Here, we detail our program structure and provide a framework for further expansion of nuclear oncology medical physics training. The fellowship is offered in partnership with three institutions: a large, tertiary community cancer center (hub site), a radiopharmaceutical research institution encompassing GMP isotope and radiopharmaceutical production and clinical and pre-clinical imaging, and a medical physics consulting group. The curriculum is split into twelve rotations covering the core competencies outlined by major certifying bodies. Primary mentors hold board certifications in diagnostic, nuclear medicine, or therapeutic medical physics. The fellowship may be completed before or after physics residency training, and culminates in a final project, in which the trainee designs a mock theranostics department. The program was verified to meet current training requirements for board certification in nuclear medicine physics. At the time of writing, the program enrolled its first fellow (pre-residency) and recruited its second trainee (post-residency). The fellowship provides a pathway for QMPs to gain the necessary training to support new theranostics programs. The curriculum may be adapted to accommodate the interests of each trainee and extended to support individuals in other crucial professions within the theranostics space. Future development of RPT-specific training guidelines may influence adjustments to the curriculum and certification processes; however, the current model provides a robust template for necessary QMP training.

papers.abstract: To assess the global and country-level greenhouse gas emissions implications of external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) scale-up to 2050. We conducted a country-level, scenario-based study across 181 countries to estimate EBRT-associated greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 and project emissions to 2050 under utilisation benchmarks of 50% and 64%, uniform schedules of 25, 15, and 5 fractions per course, and prespecified income-stratified Moderate and Ambitious hypofractionation pathways. Country-specific utilisation was examined as an access-constrained sensitivity scenario. Across all scenarios, global EBRT-associated emissions increased from 2022 to 2050. With 25-fraction delivery, emissions rose from 43.02 to 67.94 MtCO2e under the 50% utilisation and from 55.06 to 86.96 MtCO2e under the 64% utilisation. Under the 50% benchmark, 15- and 5-fraction schedules reduced 2050 emissions to 40.76 and 13.59 MtCO2e, respectively. Emissions shifted towards middle-income settings: the high-income share declined from 42.9% to 36.5%, while the 10 countries with the largest modelled EBRT-associated emissions still accounted for 64.5% of global emissions in 2022 and 60.6% in 2050. Compared with a uniform 25-fraction baseline, the Moderate pathway reduced global emissions by 23.3% in 2022 and 21.9% in 2050, while the Ambitious pathway reduced emissions by 36.5% and 34.7%, respectively. The largest absolute reductions occurred in high-income and upper-middle-income settings. Global EBRT-associated emissions are projected to rise substantially by 2050. Clinically appropriate hypofractionation offers a high-leverage mitigation opportunity, with priorities differing between decarbonising established high-volume systems and embedding low-carbon delivery during capacity expansion.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The differentiation of endometrial cancer from non-malignant endometrial findings remains clinically important. We evaluated serum human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), clinical and ultrasound features, and two published diagnostic models, the Risk of Endometrial Malignancy (REM) score and Model A. Methods: In this prospective cohort, 110 women with abnormal uterine bleeding and/or ultrasound abnormalities underwent HE4 testing, transvaginal ultrasonography, and hysteroscopy with histopathological assessment. Original univariable analyses were supplemented by reanalysis of the individual study records, including ROC metrics, paired comparisons of AUCs, and an exploratory logistic model adjusting for age and endometrial thickness. Results: Endometrial cancer was diagnosed in 18 women; 92 had non-malignant findings. Median HE4 was higher in the cancer group (118.35 versus 52.3 pmol/L; p < 0.001, as originally reported). The AUC (95% bootstrap CI) was 0.834 (0.686–0.951) for HE4, 0.905 (0.794–0.981) for REM, and 0.840 (0.702–0.948) for Model A. AUC differences were not statistically significant (paired DeLong tests, all p > 0.10). In an exploratory adjusted analysis, each doubling of HE4 was associated with higher odds of malignancy (adjusted OR 5.41; 95% CI 1.81–16.21; p = 0.0025). Conclusions: HE4 and both published models discriminated between malignant and non-malignant findings in this selected cohort. The findings are exploratory and require independent validation before clinical use.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Combining omics layers is widely expected to improve cancer drug response prediction, but this is rarely tested under family-wise error control or on an independent screen. We measured what somatic mutation and copy number data add to gene expression, and how well models transfer to unseen lineages and an external screen. Methods: We linked the Cancer Dependency Map transcriptomic, somatic mutation and copy number profiles to GDSC2 dose–response data for twelve mechanistically diverse anticancer compounds in 509 cell lines. Lineage-only, single-modality, early-fusion and stacked late-fusion gradient-boosting models were compared by repeated cross-validation (DeLong tests, Holm adjustment), leave-one-lineage-out transfer across eleven solid tumour histologies, and external validation on 77-163 held-out PRISM cell lines per compound. Results: Gene expression models outperformed tissue-of-origin baselines for all twelve agents (AUC 0.69–0.84; gains 0.024–0.169; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001 for seven drugs). Adding mutation and copy number data changed AUC by −0.015 to +0.035, and no per-drug gain survived multiplicity correction. Pooled across compounds, early fusion added 0.008 AUC (95% CI 0.000–0.016), a gain that fold-level re-analysis did not support. Mixed-lineage cross-validation exceeded leave-one-lineage-out AUC by a median of 0.030 (p = 0.0005). External PRISM AUCs ranged from 0.46 to 0.76 and followed the concordance between the two screens (Spearman rho = 0.72, p = 0.008). TreeSHAP attributions recovered known determinants, including SLFN11, TP53, BRAF, PIK3CA and downstream MAPK transcriptional effectors. Conclusions: In this twelve-drug panel, gene expression captured most of the predictable response variation. Accuracy fell on held-out lineages and on an independent screen, which sets empirical limits on how far these models can generalise.

papers.abstract: Background: Radiation segmentectomy (RS) is the selective trans-arterial delivery of an ablative dose of radiation to tumor-bearing hepatic segments, with the goal of complete tumor necrosis comparable to resection or thermal ablation. The technique was first described in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). RS has since been applied to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) and to liver metastases of diverse origin, including colorectal, neuroendocrine, breast and sarcoma primaries. Purpose: To synthesize the original-data evidence base for RS across tumor types, to demonstrate the impact of tumor vascularity on tumor-specific dosimetry methods, and to define where the evidence supports standardization of methodology. Findings: Evidence is strongest for HCC, where pathologic-explant studies tie ablative dose thresholds to complete pathologic necrosis and prospective and large-cohort data demonstrate high response rates and extended patient survival. For colorectal liver metastases, several studies have associated tumor absorbed dose with response and local control. A single study additionally suggests that the dose delivered to the peritumoral margin is associated with local tumor control, an interesting hypothesis that requires further prospective validation. Data in iCCA and neuroendocrine metastases support feasibility and durable responses. The first international dosimetry consensus for non-HCC indications appeared in 2025. Heterogeneity in dosimetry models, dose thresholds, patient selection, and outcome reporting limits cross-study pooling. Conclusions: RS serves as a potentially curative locoregional therapy for selected patients with early-stage HCC and represents a promising treatment option for non-HCC tumors, especially for those not amenable to resection or thermal ablation. Histology-specific dosimetry, prospective validation, especially in non-HCC disease, and consensus reporting standards are necessary.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Metronomic cyclophosphamide (MCP) is sometimes used for advanced soft-tissue sarcoma (STS) when standard therapies are unsuitable. We assessed its activity and safety in routine practice. Methods: This French three-center retrospective study included 60 adults with unresectable or metastatic STS who started MCP in 2008–2021. Patients received oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg twice daily on days 1–7 of 14-day cycles; 12 (20%) also received prednisolone during treatment weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Results: Median age was 70 years; 55% had ECOG performance status 2–3. Median PFS and overall survival (OS) were 2.6 months (95% CI, 1.8–3.6) and 6.4 months (95% CI, 4.2–9.3), respectively. The objective response rate was 5.0% (3/60; exact 95% CI, 1.0–13.9%) and the disease control rate was 21.7% (13/60; exact 95% CI, 12.1–34.2%); ten patients (16.7%) were not radiologically evaluable. In 21 patients aged >65 years treated in the first- or second-line setting, median PFS and OS were 3.2 and 7.7 months. Treatment-related adverse events were documented in 16 patients (26.7%), with no grade ≥3 events recorded. Conclusions: Intermittent low-dose MCP showed limited antitumor activity but favorable clinician-documented short-term tolerability in this multicenter cohort. Alongside prospective evidence, the results do not support routine use in unselected patients. MCP may retain an individualized palliative role when established systemic therapy is unsuitable.

papers.abstract: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) are genetically complex mesenchymal tumors with limited therapeutic options. BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1), a deubiquitinase, is a critical regulator of chromatin architecture, DNA repair, and cell cycle control. While BAP1 alterations are well-characterized in mesothelioma and uveal melanoma, their role in STS remains understudied. Increasing evidence shows BAP1 alterations are associated with STS. This review summarizes current evidence on BAP1 biology and its emerging significance in sarcoma. We discuss BAP1’s molecular functions, including its role in the Polycomb Repressive Deubiquitinase (PR-DUB) complex, and summarize recent findings implicating BAP1 loss in multiple subtypes of STS. We highlight mechanistic links between BAP1 deficiency, genomic instability, and tumor progression, and explore therapeutic implications such as polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) inhibition and epigenetic modulation. Understanding BAP1-driven pathways in STS may uncover novel biomarkers and targeted strategies, addressing a critical unmet need in sarcoma management.

papers.abstract: Posterior lumbar plexus block provides reliable anesthesia but is technically challenging and associated with risks related to deep paraspinal needle placement. Existing anterior approaches provide variable lumbar plexus coverage, and the anatomical pathways by which newer iliopsoas-based techniques reach individual plexus branches remain incompletely defined. This feasibility study evaluated whether an anterior inferior, trans-psoas injection targeting the posterior epimysium of the psoas muscle could provide a direct anterior pathway toward the lumbar plexus. A cadaveric dye study was performed on four GreenMBalmed cadaver hips. Under ultrasound guidance in the supine position, 30 mL of 0.1% methylene blue was injected in a caudal-to-cranial trajectory along the posterior epimysium of the psoas. Layered dissections assessed dye spread relative to the psoas, thoracolumbar fascia, and lumbar plexus nerves. Cranial and anterior fascial spread was observed in all four hips, with dye tracking anterior to the quadratus lumborum and extending toward the 12th rib and perinephric region. Dense staining of the lateral femoral cutaneous and iliohypogastric nerves was seen in all hips. The femoral nerve demonstrated predominantly moderate staining, while obturator nerve involvement was variable. Minimal intramuscular staining of the psoas was observed, suggesting preferential spread along fascial planes. Anterior inferior injection along the posterior epimysium of the psoas produced spread toward lumbar plexus regions in all four hips, in this limited cadaveric sample, suggesting this plane warrants further investigation. Clinical studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of this approach.

papers.abstract: Processed electroencephalography (pEEG) provides quantitative indices for monitoring anesthetic depth and is recommended in international guidelines. Prior meta-analyses have assessed EEG-guided anesthesia but none have evaluated available evidence stratified by pEEG technology. We performed a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults undergoing surgical, endoscopic, or dental procedures comparing pEEG-guided with non-pEEG-guided anesthesia. Primary outcomes were anesthetic drug use (TIVA and volatile agents) and postoperative delirium (POD ≤10 days). Secondary outcomes were extubation time, wake-up time, time to orientation, and post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay. Searches (PubMed Central, MEDLINE) were conducted on 11 April 2025; the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251067170). Random-effects models produced standardized mean differences (SMD), mean differences (MD), and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). Eighty-seven RCTs (30,611 patients; 13,586 pEEG; 17,025 non-pEEG) were included. pEEG significantly reduced propofol use (SMD -0.42, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.10; p = 0.01) and volatile anesthetic use (SMD -1.27, 95% CI -1.88 to -0.66; p < 0.01). The risk of POD decreased by 27% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.84; p < 0.01). Efficiency outcomes favored pEEG: extubation time (MD -2.90 min, 95% CI -3.64 to -2.16; p < 0.01), wake-up time (MD -1.83 min, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.25; p < 0.01), time to orientation (MD -4.11 min, 95% CI -6.99 to -1.23; p < 0.01), and PACU length of stay (MD -2.81 min, 95% CI -4.66 to -0.96; p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses suggested benefits were most consistently observed for BIS; estimates for Entropy and SEDLine were less precise due to fewer studies. Heterogeneity was substantial for several outcomes. Across 87 RCTs, pEEG-guided monitoring utilizing multiple device types improved perioperative efficiency and reduced POD compared with not using pEEG. Evidence is strongest for BIS; further well-reported trials are needed to delineate device-specific effects.

papers.abstract: Türkiye has one of the highest intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacities among middle-income countries but also globally. Nevertheless, little is known about the characteristics of ICUs in Türkiye, their temporal trends, and ICU admissions and readmissions. We sought to analyze the structural characteristics of all adult ICUs and the clinical profiles of ICU admissions across Türkiye. We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study using data from the Turkish Ministry of Health National Electronic Database. We analyzed adult ICU admissions across all levels and types over 6 years (2018-2023) and documented patient demographics, comorbidities, admission diagnoses, and ICU outcomes. We retrieved data on 3,362,539 ICU admissions. Among 22 ICU types, mixed ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of admissions (31.4%), followed by coronary (23.7%), anesthesiology (14.3%), medical (6.1%), and surgical (6.0%) ICUs. The proportion of mixed ICU beds decreased from 44.0% in 2018 to 25.1% in 2023. Most ICU beds were in state (public) hospitals (50.8%), followed by private hospitals (34.8%). The number of ICU beds increased from 2019, with a notable rise in state hospitals after 2020. The average number of ICU admissions was 659 per 100,000 population annually. The median patient age was 65 [interquartile range, 39-91] yr, and the ICU mortality was 15.5%. The leading admission diagnoses were respiratory failure (10.1%), cerebrovascular disease (7.1%), and acute kidney injury (5.2%). Hypertension (67.5%) and coronary artery disease (44.8%) were common comorbidities, particularly in nonsurvivors. The 7-day ICU readmission rate was 3.0%. The present comprehensive analysis of ICU admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023 highlights a shift toward specialization with a decrease in mixed ICUs. The impact of ICU diversity on resource use and patient outcomes requires further evaluation.

papers.abstract: Chronic inferior vena cava (IVC) stenosis is an uncommon yet serious vascular complication that can significantly impact the success of liver transplantation. We report a case in which postreperfusion venovenous bypass (VVB) was used as a temporizing strategy to achieve hemodynamic stabilization in the setting of severe hepatic venous congestion caused by a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction. A 58-yr-old male with a history of orthotopic liver transplantation complicated by recurrent IVC stenosis and end-stage kidney disease underwent a simultaneous liver and kidney transplant. Intraoperatively, dense fibrosis was encountered proximal to the suprahepatic IVC, preventing resection of the stenotic segment. Although the liver graft was successfully implanted and reperfused, severe hepatic congestion and refractory hemodynamic instability developed. Venovenous bypass was initiated to augment venous return and stabilize systemic hemodynamics. The kidney transplant was aborted owing to the patient's instability. Postoperatively, the patient initially tolerated the procedure, however, he ultimately died in the intensive care unit. This case illustrates an unconventional postreperfusion application of VVB as a rescue measure for refractory hemodynamic instability. Given the presence of a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction, VVB only provided temporary hemodynamic support and did not result in graft recovery. This underscores the physiologic limitations of VVB in the presence of irreversible mechanical outflow obstruction and highlights the importance of early recognition and surgical adaptability in anatomically complex cases.

papers.abstract: Background: Many clinicians monitor the abductor digiti minimi (ADM) muscle during surgery using electromyography (EMG) for ease and consistency of electrode placement, while practice guidelines recommend monitoring of responses at the adductor pollicis (AP) muscle. This study compared the onset time of rocuronium neuromuscular block and the sugammadex-induced recovery time recorded simultaneously from the AP and ADM muscles. Methods: In 44 consenting patients undergoing general anesthesia, simultaneous EMG recording of ADM and AP muscles was performed. Right- and left-hand selection of monitored muscle (AP vs . ADM) was randomized, and patients’ handedness was recorded. The primary outcomes were the onset time of neuromuscular block (administration of rocuronium until train-of-four [TOF] count equal to 0), recovery time (time from sugammadex administration until TOF ratio greater than or equal to 0.9), and time to maximal recovery (sugammadex administration until TOF ratio equal to 1.0). Results: There were no significant differences between ADM and AP measurements in onset time, recovery to TOF ratio greater than or equal to 0.9, or time to maximal recovery (TOF ratio equal to 1.0) between EMG responses recorded simultaneously from ADM and AP muscles. However, a difference in recovery times between ADM and AP existed, depending on which hand was monitored. When ADM was monitored on the right hand, the readings showed earlier recovery than AP, and the mean difference was 93 s (25% faster) and 105 s (20% faster) for time to TOF ratio greater than or equal to 0.9 and time to TOF ratio equal to 1.0, respectively. There was no difference between the AP and ADM muscles when monitoring was performed on the left hand. Conclusions: The current study underscores the equivalency between ADM and AP muscles for routine neuromuscular monitoring during surgery. When monitoring the nondominant arm, the ADM and AP muscles have similar recoveries. In the dominant arm, the ADM muscle recovery is significantly faster than that of the AP muscle.

papers.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia ( 145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

papers.abstract: Fluid accumulation in surgical patients is associated with worse outcomes. Lung ultrasound (LUS) and venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading can assess congestion and thereby fluid tolerance. However, evidence regarding epidemiology, feasibility, and associations of reduced fluid tolerance with outcomes in surgical patients is lacking. This was a prospective single-centre observational cohort study in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery. LUS and VExUS were performed before surgery and daily for up to 5 days after surgery. Reduced fluid tolerance was defined as pulmonary congestion (B profile on LUS), systemic congestion (VExUS ≥2), or both. The primary outcome was the prevalence of reduced fluid tolerance. Secondary outcomes were feasibility of ultrasound assessments, Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications, and length of stay (LOS). Of the 200 participants included, 73 (37%) exhibited signs of reduced fluid tolerance, most commonly on postoperative day 4 (n=28; 14%). Reduced fluid tolerance was primarily driven by pulmonary congestion (n=69; 95%), whereas systemic congestion was rare. In most affected patients (47 of 73; 64%), reduced fluid tolerance was limited to 1 day. Of 1200 planned assessments, 146 (12%) were missing: 123 because participants declined, mostly owing to the burden of repeated assessments, and 23 (2%) because of incomplete views. Reduced fluid tolerance was associated with LOS of >7 days (odds ratio 3.29; 95% CI 1.03-10.70), but not with major postoperative complications (hazard ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.49-2.86). Reduced fluid tolerance detected by ultrasound is common after major gastrointestinal surgery and associated with increased LOS. Ultrasound assessments were technically feasible, but repeated assessments were perceived as a burden by a substantial proportion of patients. NCT06166719 (principal investigator: A.P.J. Vlaar; first registered: 04-12-2023).

papers.abstract: To determine whether injection pressure and pressure-time characteristics can discriminate potentially hazardous needle-tip locations during peripheral nerve injection. Systematic review of experimental preclinical studies with narrative synthesis. Animal, ex vivo biological nerve, and human cadaver models of peripheral nerve injection. Needle placement and injection at intraneural, intrafascicular, perineural, or extraneural locations. CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 28, 2026 and updated on September 19, 2026. Studies reporting opening, peak, or plateau pressure or pressure-time characteristics in relation to anatomically defined needle-tip location were eligible. Human clinical studies and non-biological bench models were excluded. Risk of bias was evaluated using SYRCLE for animal studies and a domain-based framework for cadaveric studies. Because of substantial heterogeneity in experimental models, injection techniques, and pressure definitions, meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria: 12 animal or animal ex vivo studies and 16 human cadaver studies. Intraneural injection was generally associated with higher peak and plateau pressures than perineural injection, but substantial overlap occurred across needle locations. Importantly, low pressure did not reliably rule out intraneural injection, while elevated pressure was also observed during needle-nerve contact and fascial injection. Consequently, the commonly proposed 15-psi threshold showed inconsistent sensitivity across experimental settings. Lower thresholds, including 12 psi, appeared more sensitive in some models but have not been clinically validated. Beyond absolute pressure values, the rate of pressure rise and pressure-time curve morphology showed potential for differentiating needle-tip locations. Injection pressure monitoring may provide a nonspecific warning of needle placement within or against a poorly compliant structure. However, preclinical evidence alone cannot establish whether it should be used routinely or whether it reduces nerve injury. No universal pressure threshold or clinically recommended injection rate can currently be defined.

papers.abstract: Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P<0.001 for noninferiority); per-protocol results were consistent. Hypotensive burden below a mean arterial pressure threshold of 65 mm Hg was lower in the remimazolam group (median, 0 vs 7.5 mm Hg min; P<0.001), and tracheal extubation in the operating room was more frequent (85.2% vs 67.3%). Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

papers.abstract: Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation serves as a neuromodulation therapy that modulates neural activity to provide therapeutic benefit, particularly pain relief. This study investigated the effectiveness of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation as a minimally invasive approach for achieving pain relief. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from database inception till September 10, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults comparing short-term peripheral nerve stimulation with sham stimulation or usual care. The primary outcome was the change in average pain intensity during the implantation period. Eight RCTs (543 participants) were included. Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in average pain intensity during the implantation period at 1-4 weeks (SMD = -0.48, 95% CI = -0.71 to -0.26, P < 0.0001) and 5-8 weeks (SMD = -0.96, 95% CI = -1.22 to -0.70, P < 0.0001), but no significant result after electrode removal. For worst pain intensity, the intervention group showed a greater reduction than the control group at all time periods except 1-4 weeks after EOT. Improvements in pain interference were delayed, becoming significant at 5-8 weeks during the implantation period (MD = -1.34, 95% CI = -1.86 to -0.82, P < 0.00001) and ≥8 weeks after the end of treatment (MD = -1.09, 95%CI = -1.69 to -0.50, P = 0.0003). Subgroup analyses showed improvements in postoperative pain. The usual care-controlled subgroup showed more pronounced and sustained benefits than the sham-controlled subgroup, and the chronic pain subgroup also showed more pronounced and sustained benefits compared to the acute/subacute pain subgroup. This meta-analysis provided preliminary evidence that short-term peripheral nerve stimulation may relieve pain during the implantation period, but not all outcomes suggest sustained improvements after electrode removal. papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Non‐pharmacological interventions are essential to reduce procedural anxiety in pediatric care. Fidget and sensory toys are widely used for distraction and self‐regulation, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented. This scoping review mapped the evidence on fidget and sensory toys across general pediatric settings, with a focus on perioperative outcomes—such as anxiety, distress, and pain—to highlight relevant gaps in care. Methods This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA‐ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL, complemented by trial registries, gray literature, citation tracking, and reference screening. Studies involving children (0–18 years) evaluating fidget or sensory toys in any setting were eligible. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction. Findings Fifteen studies published between 2017 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Fidget spinners were the most frequently investigated device ( n = 9), followed by stress balls ( n = 3). Studies were conducted in educational ( n = 8) and healthcare settings ( n = 7). Educational studies generally reported limited or no benefits for attention, engagement, behavior, or academic performance. In contrast, healthcare studies generally suggested reductions in anxiety, pain, fear, and procedural distress, although findings were heterogeneous, and outcome measures varied substantially. Conclusions Current evidence does not support the routine use of fidget toys to improve attention or academic performance in educational settings. Evidence from healthcare and procedural settings suggests that fidget and sensory toys may be feasible distraction tools for selected pediatric patients, but evidence is insufficient to support routine perioperative use. Further high‐quality randomized controlled trials are needed to establish standardized intervention protocols and identify the pediatric populations and clinical settings most likely to benefit.

papers.abstract: Late motor responses, including F-waves and H-reflexes, are commonly recorded during electrophysiological diagnostic evaluation in awake patients. Although these responses could offer added value during intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, their use has not yet been widely adopted. This systematic review aims to assess current knowledge on how anesthetic and surgical factors influence the recording and monitoring of spinal late responses during surgery. The authors searched PubMed and EMBASE for relevant articles on studies of late response recording. Studies were considered eligible if the influence of one or more of the following parameters on late responses were assessed: (1) ventilation and metabolic parameters, (2) volatile agents, (3) intravenous agents, (4) neuromuscular blocking agents, (5) epidural or intrathecal agents, or (6) surgical factors. The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability. Sixty-two studies were included. Respiratory conditions like hypercapnia reduced H-reflex amplitude, whereas hyperoxia and intermittent hypoxia had limited impact. Volatile agents, including isoflurane, sevoflurane, and nitrous oxide decreased late response amplitudes, with dose-dependent effects. Most intravenous anesthetics, particularly propofol, reduced H-reflex amplitude and F-wave persistence in a dose-dependent manner. Conversely, ketamine was found to increase H-reflex amplitude. During spinal and vascular surgeries, H-reflex monitoring proved feasible and provided valuable supplementary data to the conventional motor evoked potential (MEP) and somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) modalities. This systematic review demonstrates that H-reflexes and F-waves are significantly influenced by anesthetic factors. The reviewed studies indicate that intravenous and volatile anesthetics significantly affect late responses, by reducing H-reflex and F-wave amplitudes, whereas latencies appear unaffected. The methodological quality varied significantly across the included studies and affects the interpretation of their conclusions. These findings support the potential integration of late response monitoring into intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) protocols, provided that anesthetic management and surgical context are carefully considered.

papers.abstract: Chronic postsurgical pain after thoracoscopic surgery remains common. We investigated whether perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion would reduce chronic pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection. In this multicentre, randomised controlled trial, 914 adults were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either esketamine or normal saline. Esketamine was administered as a 0.1 mg kg-1 bolus at induction, followed by continuous intraoperative infusion (0.1 mg kg-1 h-1) and postoperative infusion (0.015 mg kg-1 h-1) for 48 h. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months, defined as persistent pain with a numeric rating scale score ≥1 during coughing in the surgical region. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain, supplemental analgesics use, recovery of bowel function, in-hospital adverse events, and esketamine-related side-effects. We analysed 873 patients (median age, 55 yr; 63% female). The incidence of 3 month chronic pain was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (14.7% vs 21.2%; adjusted odds ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence interval, 0.43-0.90; P=0.013). A reduction was also observed when using a post hoc outcome definition of a numeric rating scale pain score ≥3 during coughing at 3 months (adjusted odds ratio, 0.39; 95% confidence interval, 0.19-0.84; P=0.015). Esketamine also reduced overall pain scores at rest and during coughing within the first 48 h, and decreased supplemental analgesic requirements within 48 h and 3 months. Perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion significantly reduced 3 month chronic pain after thoracoscopic lung resection without increasing adverse effects. ChiCTR2000040012. This trial was registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Identifier: ChiCTR2000040012; principal investigator: Fu-hai Ji; dated November 18, 2020; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=62319).

papers.abstract: Periprocedural anticoagulant management requires balancing thrombotic risk against procedure-specific bleeding risk. Existing procedure bleeding risk classifications are fragmented across specialties, inconsistent in methodology, and rarely extend beyond a few procedural domains, limiting their clinical applicability. To develop a comprehensive, standardized, procedure-specific bleeding risk classification to accompany the 2026 GIHP-SFAR periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines. A formal multidisciplinary consensus was conducted under the auspices of GIHP and SFAR, in collaboration with 24 surgical and interventional specialty societies. For each procedural domain, a working group performed a systematic literature review. Procedures were classified into four tiers: no bleeding risk, low bleeding risk, high bleeding risk, and very high bleeding risk. A specific category was created for procedures carrying particular contextual risk (e.g., anatomical site, patient factors, or need for reversible anticoagulation). Consensus was reached by the full expert panel. Twenty-four procedural domains were classified, ranging from regional anaesthesia and digestive endoscopy to cardiac surgery, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology. Each domain provides a procedure-specific bleeding risk table, with narrative supporting evidence. Procedures warranting delayed resumption of anticoagulation (≥72 hours) or use of short-acting/reversible anticoagulants are identified. The classification covers common and complex surgical scenarios, including those with limited published evidence where structured expert opinion was applied. This companion document provides clinicians with a standardized, evidence-based, procedure-specific bleeding risk framework across 24 domains to support individualized periprocedural anticoagulant decisions in daily practice.

papers.abstract: State Entropy (SE) and Surgical Pleth Index (SPI) parameters aim to optimise anaesthetic depth and intraoperative opioid administration, but their impact on postoperative complications remains unclear. Insufficient training and limited decision support may contribute to inconsistent findings. Thus, we evaluated whether tailored training to improve SE and SPI compliance reduced major postoperative complications. Adult inpatients undergoing intermediate- to high-risk noncardiac surgery were included in this prospective single-centre before-after study in France. The educational intervention and outcomes were based on the Kirkpatrick framework. All anaesthesia providers were invited to participate voluntarily in lectures and bedside training on SE and SPI monitoring. Training impact was assessed using a composite of major postoperative complications within 28 days as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included changes in monitoring practices. Among 1,623 eligible patients, 1,025 were included over a 13-month period (517 before and 508 after training). Of 202 eligible providers, 91 participated in the one-month training programme (45%). After training, simultaneous SE and SPI sensor use increased from 26% to 42% (P < 0.001), and combined SE-SPI compliance increased from 23% to 39% (P < 0.001). Major postoperative complications occurred in 66/517 patients (13%) before and 71/508 patients (14%) after training (P = 0.6). Multivariable and propensity score analyses showed no significant association between the intervention and the primary outcome. This training did not reduce the incidence of major postoperative complications, despite improvements in intraoperative monitoring practices. Future educational strategies should strengthen provider engagement and reinforcement to translate improved monitoring practices into clinical benefit. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06111248.

papers.abstract: To compare ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block with transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block on recovery quality 24 h after septorhinoplasty. Prospective, randomized, patient- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group trial. Tertiary training hospital; operating room and postoperative ward. Ninety adults aged 18 to 65 years, ASA physical status I or II, undergoing elective septorhinoplasty; 89 were analyzed. After induction of general anesthesia, patients received bilateral transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block (SPG group) or bilateral ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block (IO group), 2 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine per side. Surgical infiltration and multimodal analgesia were identical in both groups. The primary outcome was the total Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at 24 h. Secondary outcomes were QoR-15 domains, visual analog scale pain scores, rescue morphine, nausea and vomiting, anesthetic consumption, emergence agitation, edema, ecchymosis and recovery room stay. Total QoR-15 at 24 h was higher in the IO group (129.1 ± 9.4 versus 116.6 ± 11.7; mean difference 12.5 points, 95% CI 8.01 to 17.01; P = 0.001), above the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 8. More IO patients crossed the acceptable symptom state threshold of 118 (86.4% versus 35.6%; P < 0.001). Pain scores were lower at every time point and fewer IO patients needed rescue analgesia (11.4% versus 53.3%; P = 0.001). Nausea and vomiting, anesthetic consumption and recovery room stay did not differ. Infraorbital nerve block gave better 24 h patient-reported recovery than sphenopalatine ganglion block after septorhinoplasty. Secondary findings are hypothesis-generating. ClinicalTrials.govNCT06929429.

papers.abstract: Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened with a spectrum of health issues and consistently report lower satisfaction with their health care; nevertheless, little is known about their experiences with critical care and the support received during critical illness. We aimed to describe the current scope of critical-care-specific resources available to Indigenous patients and their families across Alberta to identify gaps and opportunities to implement actionable change to realize more equitable and culturally safe care. We conducted a two-phase environmental scan. Phase 1 entailed searching websites for information to support Indigenous patients, their families, and health care workers. Phase 2 facilitated 21 interviews with intensive care unit (ICU) stakeholders from across Alberta to further describe site-specific resources, services, tools, or initiatives to support Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous partners were engaged through all aspects of the project. Our environmental scan identified a paucity of ICU-specific resources, programs, or policies to support Indigenous patients and families' navigation with critical care. We identified two national resources aimed at clinicians, rather than patients or families. Interviews with ICU stakeholders confirmed the paucity of Indigenous-specific resources. Stakeholders cited numerous barriers, including inadequate culture training, staff time constraints and burnout, physical space limits, and insufficient personnel, such as Indigenous liaisons and social workers. Multiple gaps exist in the availability of critical-care-focused resources and supports for Indigenous Peoples experiencing critical illness in Alberta, Canada. Addressing these care gaps may improve health equity, access, and the experience for Indigenous patients and families during critical illness and further build trust and strengthen relationships with health care workers.

papers.abstract: Pain after kidney transplantation is often severe, and graft function constrains the use of systemic analgesia. Previous syntheses of regional techniques pooled them as a class, combined donors with recipients, and did not use a minimal clinically important difference (MCID). We searched PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL through 5 September 2026 for randomised trials of regional analgesia in adult kidney transplant recipients (PROSPERO CRD420261478933); a trial-registry search and network meta-analysis were added post hoc. Bayesian random-effects models with MCID-scaled priors yielded posterior probabilities of benefit and of exceeding the MCID, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Fourteen trials (903 participants) were included. Only quadratus lumborum (QL) and transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks could be pooled against control. Both yielded lower pain at every pooled time point, but no pairwise pain comparison reached 80% probability of exceeding the 1.0 point MCID. Opioid consumption at 24 h was lower with the QL block (-15.5 morphine milligram equivalents; 95% credible interval -23.6 to -6.7) and the TAP block (-10.5; -14.4 to -5.5), with each reduction exceeding the 5 mg MCID with a probability >97%. In the network meta-analysis, no difference between QL and TAP blocks in pain or opioid consumption reached 80% probability of exceeding the MCID. Graft function and safety data were too sparse to pool. Twelve eligible registered trials were unpublished; certainty of evidence was very low. Quadrtus lumborum and transversus abdominus plane blocks reduce pain and opioid consumption at 24 h, but only the reduction in opioid consumption has a high probability of being clinically important. Certainty of evidence is very low; no technique is preferred, and effects on graft function are unknown.

papers.abstract: Non-pharmacological techniques have recently been developed to decrease preoperative anxiety, and music or video may be combined, as in children. This study aims to compare two additional preoperative strategies in adult outpatients. This before-after trial was approved by the ethics committee and included adults undergoing ambulatory procedures under general anaesthesia. It compared usual care before surgery and another period with a video of the expected local journey combined with a relaxing music session. After consent, the level of anxiety was measured via the APAIS score, a repeated visual analogue scale for anxiety, and investigators collected preoperative fears. The main objective was to reduce the number of patients with significant preoperative anxiety. Secondary outcomes compared anxiety during the journey, pain, and quality of recovery after surgery. A P-value < 0.05 was considered significant. 99 patients were included in each period, and 194 completed the study. The intervention group showed a significant reduction in the rate of patients with significant anxiety at admission in the operating room: 23/95 (24.2%, 95%CI [16.7-33.7]) vs. 43/99 (43.4%, 95%CI [34.1-53.3]) with P = 0.005. Secondary outcomes showed no difference in anxiety after surgery, neither in length of stay nor incidence of PONV. The postoperative level of pain was also statistically reduced (P = 0.033). The study suggests that a combined video and music strategy decreases the rate of significant anxiety in patients undergoing outpatient procedures. This low-cost strategy showed a high level of satisfaction and should be encouraged in adults. Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06461052.

papers.abstract: Due to limited resources, identifying high-risk surgical patients who derive clinical benefit from Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission is essential. Our primary aim was to characterize resource allocation and evaluate the true clinical benefit of ICU admissions using modified Wang criteria. Secondary aim is to identify independent risk factors for ICU admission; validate clinical scoring systems; and compare inter-group outcomes, including Clavien-Dindo complication rates, lengths of stay, and mortality. This multicenter, prospective, observational study was conducted across 75 ICUs. Adult inpatient surgery cases were categorized into four groups: planned admission (PAG), unplanned admission (UPAG), planned but not admitted (PBNAG), and emergent admission (EAG). Data included preoperative/intraoperative/postoperative(ICU) variables, modified Wang criteria, and mortality rates (ICU, hospital, 30/90-day). Of 55,963 preoperatively evaluated patients, 2764 (4.9%) were planned for ICU admission; 804/2764 patients could not be admitted because of limited ICU beds, remaining of 1960 patients with a planned ICU admission, 411/1960 did not require postoperative ICU care forming the PBNAG (14.8% of 2764). Overall, 1980 patients (3.09% of all cases) were admitted to the ICU (78.2% PAG, 12.5% EAG, 9.1% UPAG). POSSUM scores effectively differentiated PBNAG (lower) and EAG (higher) from PAG. ICU benefit indicators (e.g., vasopressor need, prolonged ventilation >12 h, arrest events) were significantly higher in UPAG and EAG versus PAG (p 2 (OR 2.7) independently increased UPAG risk, whereas minimally invasive surgery and regional anesthesia reduced ICU admissions. Overall ICU and 90-day mortality rates were 5.9% and 7.5%, respectively, peaking in the EAG group (18.1% and 18.9%). Integrating modified Wang criteria, POSSUM scores, intraoperative complications, emergency status, and ASA class >2 is effective in predicting the necessity of ICU admission.

papers.abstract: Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min). Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

papers.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is an important postoperative neurocognitive complication, and cumulative anticholinergic drug burden (ADB) may increase its risk by impairing central cholinergic neurotransmission. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the overall association between ADB scores and POD risk in adult surgical patients. We searched major databases and trial registries through February 2026 for studies that assessed ADB using validated scales and reported POD outcomes in adult surgical patients. Random-effects models pooled SMDs and ORs. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored heterogeneity and robustness. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS, and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Ten reports from nine independent cohorts comprising 10,457 participants were included. Patients with POD had higher ADB scores than those without POD (SMD = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.20-0.43). Each one-point increase in continuous ADB was associated with 22% higher odds of POD (OR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.09-1.37). Both low-to-moderate and high burden were associated with increased POD risk. In scale-specific analyses, the association was significant for ACB. The association was attenuated in studies that excluded patients with cognitive impairment. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high, and certainty of evidence was low. Higher ADB is significantly associated with higher odds of POD, with a graded increase in risk across burden levels. Baseline cognitive impairment appears to amplify this association. These findings support preoperative ADB assessment and medication optimization in vulnerable surgical patients, while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head comparisons of anticholinergic burden scales. papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains one of the most common serious complications after noncardiac surgery, and intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is consistently identified as a modifiable risk factor. Observational studies show a consistent, roughly dose-response association between IOH, particularly at mean arterial pressures below 60-65 mmHg, and postoperative AKI, with stronger associations in patients with limited renal reserve. Definitions of IOH vary widely, which complicates the comparison of studies and the translation of thresholds into clinical targets. Randomized trials of individualized or higher blood pressure targets have generally not confirmed a kidney-protective benefit, and pooled analyses with trial sequential analysis have not demonstrated that higher targets reduce AKI. This narrative review examines how IOH definitions evolved, summarizes the conflicting intervention evidence, and assesses the controversies that shape current practice. The review concludes that avoiding severe and sustained hypotension remains reasonable, whereas current randomized trial evidence does not support a general kidney-protective benefit of higher or individualized blood pressure targets. This conclusion is provisional and is tempered by the methodologic and causal uncertainties.

papers.abstract: Tracheal intubation is a physically and mentally demanding for anesthesiologists because it requires fine motor control, technical precision, rapid decision-making, situational awareness, and error avoidance. While videolaryngoscopes reduce muscle strain in normal airways, their ergonomic impact during difficult airway management remains poorly established. We aimed to compare upper limb muscle activity using dynamic surface electromyography during intubation via direct laryngoscopy (DL) vs videolaryngoscopy (VL) in simulated difficult airway scenarios. We conducted a randomized crossover trial involving 35 experienced anesthesiologists who performed tracheal intubation on a high-fidelity manikin with a normal airway, locked jaw, and rigid neck, respectively, using a Macintosh direct laryngoscope, a C-MAC® videolaryngoscope (C blade), and a King Vision® channeled videolaryngoscope. The primary outcome was upper limb muscle activity, measured by surface electromyography. Secondary outcomes included intubation time, force on upper incisors, first-attempt success rate, and perceived workload (National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index [NASA-TLX] score). Direct laryngoscopy produced significantly higher brachioradialis muscle activity than C-MAC VL in the simulated normal airway (16 vs 13 µV; median difference [MD], 3 µV; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0 to 5; P = 0.04), locked jaw (18 vs 12 µV; MD, 6 µV; 95% CI, 1 to 11; P = 0.02), and rigid neck (16 vs 13 µV; MD, 4 µV; 95% CI, 0 to 9; P = 0.03) scenarios. Direct laryngoscopy was the fastest method but exerted the highest force on the incisors (P < 0.001). King Vision VL was associated with the highest NASA-TLX workload score (P < 0.001 compared with DL), whereas C-MAC VL was least demanding. In simulated difficult airways, VL reduced upper limb muscle activity compared with DL. Nevertheless, perceived workload was higher with King Vision VL than with DL, whereas it was lower with C-MAC VL. Among the devices tested, C-MAC VL provided the most favorable ergonomic balance, combining reduced muscle strain, lower perceived workload, and highest first-attempt success rate across all airway scenarios. papers.abstract: Scoliosis surgery is complex and associated with significant morbidity. Accurate risk assessment is essential for appropriate resource allocation and improved care. Risk factors for developing complications have been identified; however, structured frameworks to support preoperative assessment are limited. Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) uses a three-tier multidisciplinary team (MDT) traffic-light system to triage patients based on well-defined risk factors and expert clinical judgment. We aimed to describe complications following scoliosis surgery at GOSH and evaluate the relationship between preoperative MDT traffic-light assessment and outcomes such as complication rates, operative times, and length of stay. A retrospective hospital file review was conducted for all patients presenting to GOSH for primary scoliosis surgery between January 2019 and December 2023. Institutional approval was obtained, and the need for ethical approval was waived. Preoperative risk is quantified by the MDT using a three-tier traffic-light system categorizing patients as low (green), intermediate (amber), and high-risk (red). Outcomes including 30-day in-hospital complications, operative time, and length of stay were analyzed in relation to preoperative MDT traffic-light score. Of 350 eligible patients, 337 had a documented preoperative MDT traffic-light assessment. Low-risk patients comprised 43.6% (n = 147/337), intermediate-risk 49.3% (n = 166/337), and high-risk 7.1% (n = 24/337). Major complications occurred in 2% (n = 3/147) of low-risk patients compared with 50% (n = 12/24) of high-risk patients, corresponding to an adjusted odds ratio of 11.4 ([95% CI 1.98-65.4], p = 0.006). High-risk patients also had significantly longer operative times (381 min vs. 320 min, p < 0.001) and length of stay (12 days vs. 5 days, p < 0.001) when compared to low-risk patients. Patients classified as high-risk by the MDT demonstrated an increased odds of developing major complications, longer operative time, and extended length of stay when compared to low-risk patients. Similar structured tools, with local adaptations, may be valuable in other centers to support preoperative assessment, shared decision making, and guide resource allocation.

papers.abstract: Patients referred for postoperative care within enhanced care units in the United Kingdom are less likely to have their surgery canceled than those referred to critical care. Presently, it is unclear whether this association remains when examined at an individual hospital level, and whether specific structure and process features of enhanced care services influence cancelation rates within a facility. We conducted a nationwide, retrospective, observational study documenting clinical and organizational features of enhanced and critical care facilities in the United Kingdom. Features of interest included resource protections, staffing, and clinical scope. Sites with availability of both enhanced and critical care facilities, with >10 referrals to enhanced care during the study period, were selected for analysis. Cancelation rates of elective surgery within these facilities were quantified over a 3-month period between September 1, 2023, and November 30, 2023. Rates were defined as the number of elective cases canceled divided by the number of elective referrals to each facility. Multilevel regression was used to explore relationships between structure and process features of enhanced care units and surgical cancelation, using a two-level model with cases nested within hospitals to account for institutional confounding. Complete data were available for 65 sites, of which 28 had an enhanced care facility with sufficient activity for analysis, representing 4112 patients referred to enhanced or critical care. In most institutions, surgical cancelation rates were lower within their enhanced care facility than in critical care. Enhanced care units with beds reserved exclusively for elective cases (odds ratio [OR], 0.54 [0.39-0.76]; P < .001) and clinical care involving multiple specialities (OR, 0.48 [0.33-0.69]; P < .001) were associated with reduced odds of cancelation. On the other hand, enhanced care units that permitted admission of emergency cases (OR, 1.61 [1.06-2.43]; P = .024) were associated with a greater odds of cancelation. Structure and process features of enhanced care pathways are associated with cancelation rates among high-risk surgical patients in the United Kingdom. These findings may explain why cancelation rates in enhanced care are typically lower than within critical care and may have important policy implications.

papers.abstract: Preoperative anxiety affects 30% to 80 % of ambulatory surgery patients and is associated with increased anesthetic requirements, postoperative pain, and delayed recovery. Virtual reality (VR) is a promising nonpharmacological anxiolytic, but evidence remains limited in the ambulatory setting. The AMBLUMEEN (AMBulatory LUMEEN) trial is a single-center, randomized, open-label, superiority trial conducted in an adult ambulatory surgery unit. Patients with moderate-to-severe preoperative anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y-A [STAI-YA] > 45) were randomized 1:1 to standard care alone (control) or standard care and a single 20-minute preoperative VR session (immersive 360° natural contemplative scenes). The primary end point was the change in STAI-YA score from arrival in the ambulatory unit (baseline) to immediately before operating room transfer (presurgery), analyzed under the intention-to-treat principle with a linear mixed model. Secondary end points included preoperative benzodiazepine use, postoperative morphine requirement, unplanned overnight admission, patient satisfaction, and device acceptability. Of 106 randomized patients (53 per group) with a median [interquartile range] baseline STAI-YA of 49 [46-55] and 49 [46-58] respectively in the control and VR group, the VR group experienced a markedly greater reduction in state anxiety than controls. Adjusted mean between-group difference in STAI-YA change from baseline to presurgery was -18.7 95% confidence interval (CI) [-21.4 to -16.1] points in favor of VR. Although benzodiazepine requirement, postoperative pain, and unplanned overnight admission were comparable between groups, the morphine requirement in postanesthesia care unit was lower in the VR group (6/53 [11.3% 95% CI, 11.3 {4.3-23.0}] vs 0/53 [0.0%, 95% CI, {0.0-6.7}]; P = .027). Global perioperative satisfaction was high in both groups (median 8 [8-9] on 10). A single 20-minute session of medical-grade VR significantly reduced preoperative anxiety in ambulatory surgery patients, with high acceptability and an excellent safety profile.

papers.abstract: Although nonpharmacological interventions are recommended for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND), cognitive training has not been explicitly advocated. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA) and meta-regression tested the hypothesis that preoperative cognitive training, compared with usual care, reduces the incidence of PND. Eight databases and two clinical trial registries were searched for RCTs comparing preoperative cognitive training with usual care. Primary outcomes were postoperative delirium (POD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (DNR), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder. Thirteen RCTs with 1446 patients were identified. Preoperative cognitive training was associated with a lower risk of POD (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.36-0.77; P = 0.001; low certainty). Subgroup analysis (P for interaction = 0.01) and meta-regression (β1 1.072, 95% CI 0.006-2.138, P = 0.049) suggested an association between training format and treatment effect on POD, with a potentially greater benefit for traditional training. For DNR, the incidence was lower in the training group than in the usual care group (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.46-0.96; P = 0.03; very low certainty), but this finding was not supported by several sensitivity analyses. No significant differences were detected between subgroups for training format, total duration, or surgery type (P for interaction = 0.06, 0.37, and 0.34, respectively), and meta-regression suggested that overall risk of bias was a potential moderator for DNR (P = 0.045). TSA suggested a potential for false-positive findings, as the cumulative Z-curves did not cross the TSA boundaries, and the required information sizes were not reached for either outcome. Preoperative cognitive training may reduce the incidence of POD, with traditional training showing a potentially greater benefit than digital training. For DNR, the current evidence is insufficient to support a preventive effect of preoperative cognitive training, although a trend toward benefit was observed. These findings are limited by high risk of bias in several included trials and failure to reach the required information sizes in TSA, particularly for DNR, which need to be confirmed in future large-scale RCTs. papers.abstract: Inflammation is widely viewed as a driver of pain, yet clinical and transcriptomic studies report conflicting associations. A clearer understanding of how inflammatory processes relate to pain across clinical contexts is essential for improving diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of chronic pain. We analysed whole-blood RNA sequencing from seven human cohorts spanning four pain conditions, including acute, postoperative, chronic localised, and chronic widespread pain in almost 500 blood samples with corresponding pain intensity scores. Using gene-level meta-analyses, pathway enrichment, and immune cell-specific gene ontologies, we tested how inflammatory responses relate to current pain, future pain trajectories, and within-person changes over time. Inflammation emerged as one of the strongest biological correlates of pain across all cohorts, yet its association direction depended on the pain state. In acute musculoskeletal and postoperative pain, higher inflammatory activation, which correlated with enhanced neutrophil and macrophage function, was associated with greater pain intensity but also correlated with better subsequent recovery, consistent with an adaptive inflammatory response. In chronic localised pain, this relationship was disrupted and inverted: higher inflammatory activity was linked to lower pain intensity and associated with worse long-term outcomes. In chronic widespread pain, macrophage-related inflammatory activity remained positively associated with both pain severity and persistence, suggesting progression toward a maladaptive immune state. These findings indicate that inflammation is not uniformly detrimental in pain but plays distinct roles depending on disease stage and context. Inflammation might support resolution during acute injury yet become dysregulated in chronic and nociplastic pain. Recognising these context-dependent roles could help explain conflicting findings in the literature and guide more precise use of anti-inflammatory therapies.

papers.abstract: Pre-operative clear fluid fasting in children aims to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration. Recent studies have shown the safety of shorter clear fluid fasting durations. However, because pulmonary aspiration is rare, it remains uncertain whether the incidence differs between the liberal (< 2 h) and conventional (≥ 2 h) clear fluid fasting policies. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, performing comprehensive searches across five databases. We included studies with patients aged < 18 y who underwent general anaesthesia or sedation for surgery or procedures. Primary outcome was pulmonary aspiration and secondary outcome was vomiting without pulmonary aspiration. We performed meta-analyses to estimate pooled incidences according to fasting policy (< 2 h vs. ≥ 2 h). We included 33 studies involving 580,197 patients. Twenty-nine studies (579,737 patients) reported pulmonary aspiration. The pooled incidence of pulmonary aspiration was 0.03% (95%CI 0.01-0.09%) with conventional fasting policies and 0.03% (95%CI 0.01-0.09%) with liberal policies. Risk ratios were available from 14 studies (475,399 patients) and showed no difference in pulmonary aspiration between policies (risk ratio 0.77, 95%CI 0.40-1.47). Seventeen studies (344,653 patients) reported vomiting; the pooled incidence was 0.99% (95%CI 0.27-3.51%) with conventional policies and 0.76% (95%CI 0.18-3.14%) with liberal policies. The certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes. Pulmonary aspiration is rare in children, and similar incidences of aspiration and vomiting were observed under liberal and conventional clear fluid fasting policies. The results should be interpreted cautiously due to the very low certainty of evidence.
